entries.narration: Java is a programming language, but it is also a promise. You write your code once, a compiler turns it into bytecode, and a Java virtual machine runs that bytecode on any computer that has one. Thirty years after it first appeared, that promise is why Java is everywhere you do not see it. On the left, Java answers a few questions about itself. The version is twenty five, a long term support release, and it is the Java this whole course runs on. The runtime lists sixty nine modules, and three of them hint at how much comes ready made: java dot base, the core of the language, java dot net dot http, for talking to web services, and java dot sql, for databases. That is a lot of code you will never have to write. On the right is what runs on the JVM. Banks and payment systems, where Java has been the default for decades, because it is fast, safe with memory, and strict about types. The web backends behind countless apps, built with frameworks like Spring Boot. Android apps. And the big data infrastructure of the internet: Kafka, which moves events between systems, Spark and Flink, which process data at scale, and Elasticsearch, which searches it. This course teaches Java by building one real application in the place Java is most at home: a bank. Not a toy that prints Hello World and stops, but a ledger that grows from a single file to a tested, packaged service that handles thousands of transfers at the same time without losing a cent. Along the way you will learn the language properly, not just what to type but what the compiler and the JVM do with it, with short detours inside whenever a question needs the answer. All you need is the JDK. Here is what we will build.

Meet Syndica Bank. It is small, it is fictional, and by the end of this course you will have written every line of it. This is its map. On the left are the requests a bank has to answer: tellers making deposits, withdrawals and transfers, statements imported from files, with some bad rows in them, and later, programs calling it over HTTP. In the middle is the ledger itself, built from parts, and each part is labelled with the course that builds it. The model, which gives the bank real types: an account, an amount of money, a transaction. The Bank, which keeps every account and every transaction. Statements, which work out balances and monthly reports. The Journal, which writes every transaction to disk, so the bank survives a restart. The TransferService, which lets ten thousand transfers run at once without losing a cent. And an API, so other programs can use the bank over the web. Along the bottom is what turns working code into professional software: a first single file, a Maven build that produces a runnable jar, and tests, logs and a look inside the JVM. On the right is what comes out: monthly statements, a journal of every transaction, and JSON responses, where a transfer that is retried still pays only once. And on the right is the payoff, taken from the very end of the course: the finished bank, really running, answering over HTTP. Ana's account comes back as JSON, and a transfer of twenty five euros is paid. The course has a simple rhythm. Each section adds one thing the bank needs, and teaches the part of Java that does it, at exactly the moment you need it: exact money when we first pay interest, classes when an account needs rules, threads when tellers start working at the same time. And every output you see comes from really running the code, on Java twenty five. Let's install a JDK.

Every Java program you will ever write starts with one download: a JDK, the Java Development Kit. Any OpenJDK 25 build will do. This one comes from Ubuntu's package manager, and on a Mac or on Windows you would install a build such as Temurin instead. Once it is installed, two questions in the terminal tell you it works. java dash dash version answers with three lines. The first says openjdk twenty five, the release this course uses. Java 25 is a long term support release, so it will be maintained for years. The third line names the virtual machine that will run our code, the OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM, better known as HotSpot. javac dash dash version answers too, with the same number. Then we ask where java actually lives. readlink follows the links from the command to the real file, and it lands inside one folder, the JDK itself, which is open in the explorer on the left. Its bin folder holds twenty nine tools. In this course we will use a handful: javac, the compiler, jshell, javap, jar, and java. In the editor is the JDK's release file, a plain description of what was installed: the version, the date it was built, and a long list of modules, folded away here. The diagram on the right is the picture to keep. The JDK is everything you need to write Java. Inside it is the runtime, which is what you need to run Java: the java launcher and the class library, sixty nine modules of ready made code. And inside the runtime is the JVM, the engine that actually runs programs, with an interpreter, a just in time compiler and a garbage collector. Each of them gets its own moment later in the course. Finally, we make a folder for the bank, called ledger, and step into it. It is empty. In the next section it gets its first file.

Syndica Bank begins as a single file, Bank dot java. Look at how little it takes. Line one starts with two slashes, which makes it a comment: a note for people that the compiler skips. Line three opens a method called main, and main is where every Java program starts. The word void says that main gives nothing back when it finishes. Older Java made you wrap this method in a class and write public static void main, with a list of arguments, before you could print a single word. Since Java 25, a file like this one, called a compact source file, can start with main itself. The class arrives later in the course, at the moment the bank needs one. Inside main are two statements, and each ends with a semicolon. Both call IO dot println, which prints a line of text to the terminal. The first prints the bank's banner. The second prints Ana's balance: a hundred and twenty euros fifty. In the terminal, java Bank dot java runs the file. The diagram on the right shows what happens in one step: the java launcher compiles the whole file in memory, and then runs main from its first line to its last. The table walks down the file. The comment does nothing, main starts, line four prints, line five prints, and when main ends, so does the program. Now look closely at line five, because the second table takes it apart. Inside the brackets, some text in quotes, a String, is joined to a number with a plus sign. When one side of a plus is a String, Java turns the other side into text and glues the two together. But notice what came out. We typed one hundred twenty point five zero, and the terminal says one hundred twenty point five. The trailing zero is gone. That number is a double, and a double keeps the value, not the way it was written. For a bank, that is already a warning sign. To see exactly where the zero went, the next section follows this file through the compiler and the JVM.

When you type java Bank dot java, two separate things happen, and here we do them one at a time, by hand, so you can see each one. Every box holds the real output of a tool that ships with the JDK. Along the top is the compile phase. Box one is the source, the text we wrote. Box two runs javac, the compiler, on it. javac prints nothing when it succeeds, but ls shows a new file beside our source: Bank dot class. That file holds no Java text at all. It holds bytecode, a compact set of instructions for the Java virtual machine, and it is the same on every operating system. That is the old promise of Java: compile once, run anywhere there is a JVM. When you run java Bank dot java directly, this step happens in memory, and no class file is left behind. Box three opens the class file with javap dash c, which lists the bytecode. main has become five instructions. Load a constant, call println, load a second constant, call println again, and return. Now look at that second constant. It is the whole sentence, Ana's balance, colon, one hundred twenty point five. The compiler saw text plus a fixed number, worked out the result itself, and stored a single string. So the trailing zero did not disappear when the line ran. It was gone before the program ever started. Along the bottom is the run phase, in box four. java Bank starts the JVM and loads classes. The log shows where each one came from: our Bank from the ledger folder, and IO from java dot base, the core module of the class library. Even this tiny program loads over four hundred classes before main finishes, most of them from a shared archive that makes startup fast. In box five, the JVM's interpreter runs the bytecode one instruction at a time. Methods that run often enough are handed to the just in time compiler, which turns them into machine code. This program finishes long before that matters. Box six is what was printed. Every Java program, however large, follows this same path.

Java has a second way to run code, and it is the one to reach for whenever you are not sure what a line will do. jshell, here with dash q for a quieter output, is Java's interactive shell. The loop on the right describes it. It reads the snippet you type, compiles and evaluates it straight away, and prints the value, without being asked. Each value even gets a name, dollar one, dollar two, so you can use it again. The bank wants to pay interest, so we try the arithmetic here first. One hundred twenty point five zero comes back as one hundred twenty point five, the same lost zero as before. Add a deposit of twenty five point one zero, and the answer, one hundred forty five point six, looks fine. Now the interest. One and a half percent of one hundred twenty point five zero should be exactly one point eight zero seven five. jshell says one point eight zero seven four nine nine nine, and a long run of nines. This is not a bug in Java. A double stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions, like zero point zero one five, have no exact binary form. The double holds the nearest value it can, and the multiplication carries the error. The table at the bottom puts jshell and the file side by side. jshell runs one snippet at a time and shows every value, but when you type slash exit, everything you tried is gone. The file runs main from top to bottom, shows only what you print, and keeps every line. So jshell is for trying, and the file is for the bank. Trying the line has done its job, so we write it into Bank dot java as line six and run the file. It prints the same long number. For a bank, that is simply the wrong answer: interest must come out in exact cents. We will leave it, deliberately, and fix it properly in the next course, with a type made for money.

Every programmer breaks their code many times a day, so one of the most useful skills you can learn is reading what Java says when it happens. Here, on line six, println has lost a letter. We run the file, and look closely at the terminal: there is no banner. Line four is perfectly correct, yet it never printed. That tells you when this error was found. Before the JVM runs a single instruction, javac compiles the whole file, and it checks much more than the grammar. It checks that every name refers to something that really exists, and that every value has the right type. The diagram on the right follows that path. The compiler could not find a method called prinln, so it produced no bytecode at all, and with no bytecode, nothing runs. Now read the error itself, with the table beside it. The first line gives the file and the line number, six, then the word error and the problem: cannot find symbol. The next line shows the code, with a caret pointing at the exact spot. Then two more lines say what the compiler looked for, a method called prinln that takes a String, and where it looked, in the class IO. Finally, the count of errors, and the launcher's own message that compilation failed. In some languages, Python for one, a typo like this is only discovered when the line runs, after everything before it has already happened. Java finds it before the program starts. That is the first payoff of a compiled, typed language, and the compiler will catch a great deal more for us as the bank grows. At the bottom is the other compile error you will meet every day, a missing semicolon. Same shape: the file, the line, what was expected, and a caret where it belongs. The habit for both is the same: read the message, go to the line it names, and look around the caret. Next, a mistake the compiler cannot see.

This time the spelling is fixed, and two new lines report an average and close the bank. Line seven divides the balance, a hundred and twenty, by the number of months the account has been open, which for a brand new account is zero. As far as the compiler is concerned, that is perfectly good Java: a number divided by a number. So the file compiles, the JVM starts, and main begins to run. The table on the right shows what happened, line by line. Lines four, five and six run, and their output appears in the terminal. Then line seven tries to divide a whole number by zero, which has no answer, and the JVM throws an exception, an ArithmeticException. Nothing catches it, so main stops right there, the program ends, and line eight, which would have closed the bank, never runs. Read the stack trace from the top. Exception in thread main: the thread that runs main, which is where it happened. Then the exception's full name, java dot lang dot ArithmeticException, and its message, slash by zero. Then the at lines, one for each method that was running, the most recent first. Here there is just one: Bank dot main, in the file Bank dot java, at line seven. In a bigger program the list is longer, and it reads like a trail back to where things went wrong. The table at the bottom is the real lesson of this pair of sections. A compile error is found by javac, before main starts, so nothing happens at all. An exception is found by the running JVM, only when it reaches the bad line, so everything before that line has already happened. Here that means three printed lines. In a bank, it could mean money taken from one account and never added to the other. That is why this course will check its input, handle its exceptions, and test its code. Remove the line, and the first program is done. In the next course, the bank starts to hold real data.

So far, every value in Bank dot java has been typed straight into the line that uses it. A real bank needs to name its values, so it can use them again. That is what a variable is: a name for a value. Look at the top of main. Each line declares a variable, and each declaration has three parts, shown at the top of the diagram: a type, a name, and a value. String bank holds the bank's name. int accounts holds a whole number, one. double balance holds Ana's balance. And the last one says var instead of a type. var asks the compiler to work out the type from the value, so rate is a double, exactly as if we had written it. The table lists all five, with the type each one has. That type is the heart of Java. It is fixed the moment the name is declared, and it never changes. The lines below use the names: bank plus colon open, holder plus apostrophe s balance. Running the file prints the bank's banner, now with a count of accounts, and the same long interest as before, because nothing about the arithmetic has changed yet. Now, what does a fixed type buy us? In jshell, we try to put the text one into an int. Java refuses, before anything runs: incompatible types, String cannot be converted to int. The caret points at the value that does not fit. In a language without static types, a mistake like that waits quietly until some later line trips over it. Here, the compiler catches it on the spot, and in a bank, where a balance that is secretly a piece of text could cost real money, that is exactly what you want. Every variable you will meet from now on has a type, so it is worth knowing what different types actually hold. That is the next section.

A variable holds a value, but what exactly is in it depends on its type, and Java has two very different kinds. The diagram on the right shows main's variables as they really sit in memory. While main runs, it has a frame on the stack: a small block of memory with one slot for each of its local variables. Look at balance and accounts. Their slots hold the values themselves, one hundred twenty point five and one. double and int are primitive types, and a primitive is nothing more than its value, stored directly in the slot. Now look at holder and bank. Their slots do not hold any text. They hold a reference, drawn as an arrow, to an object that lives somewhere else, in a large area of memory called the heap. The text Ana is a String object on the heap, and so is Syndica Bank. String is a reference type. In the terminal, jshell proves the difference. Ask holder for its length, and the String object answers: three. Ask balance for its length, and the compiler refuses: double cannot be dereferenced. Dereferencing means following an arrow to an object, and a primitive has no arrow to follow. It is just a number, with no methods to call. The table sums it up. A primitive holds the value itself. A reference holds an arrow to an object, and the object has methods. Java has exactly eight primitive types: the whole numbers byte, short, int and long, the two floating point types, float and double, a single character, char, and boolean, true or false. Every other type, String, BigDecimal, the arrays and the classes we will write, is a reference type, and its objects live on the heap. This picture comes back again and again in this course. It explains why comparing two strings can go wrong, what null means, and what the garbage collector cleans up.

Since the first course, Ana's interest has come out as one point eight zero seven four nine nine nine, and so on. It is time to understand why, and to fix it. In jshell, the most famous sum in programming: zero point one plus zero point two. The answer is zero point three zero zero zero zero, with a four at the end. Ask whether that equals zero point three, and Java says false. The diagram at the top explains it. In decimal, one tenth is exact: zero point one. But a double stores numbers in binary, and in binary one tenth is zero point zero zero zero one one zero zero one one, with the pattern repeating forever, the way one third repeats forever in decimal. A double keeps only fifty three binary digits, so it stores the nearest value it can, which is a tiny bit more than one tenth. Most amounts of money, ten cents, twelve ninety nine, have the same problem. For a bank, an amount that is almost right is wrong. One classic way out is to stop using fractions altogether, and count in whole cents. The file now does exactly that. balanceCents is a long, the sixty four bit whole number type, holding twelve thousand and fifty: one hundred twenty euros fifty. Whole numbers are exact, so adding and subtracting cents never drifts. The rate becomes fifteen per thousand. Run the file, and the balance in cents is exact. But look at the interest: one hundred and eighty cents. The true answer is one hundred eighty point seven five. Dividing one whole number by another throws away the fraction, silently, with no rounding and no warning. Cents fix adding, but the moment a bank multiplies by a rate and divides, it needs to decide exactly how to round, and a long cannot do that for us. Java has a type built for this, and it is the next section.

BigDecimal is Java's type for exact decimal numbers, and it is what banks and payment systems use for money. It lives in the java dot math package, and since a compact source file imports the whole core library for us, we can use it straight away. The balance becomes a new BigDecimal, built from the text one hundred twenty point five zero, and the rate from the text zero point zero one five. Run the file, and look at the difference. The balance prints as one hundred twenty point five zero, with its zero. Interest prints as one point eight zero seven five zero, exactly one and a half percent, with no long tail. The table on the right shows why. A BigDecimal is two whole numbers: an unscaled value, and a scale that says how many digits sit after the decimal point. One hundred twenty point five zero is twelve thousand and fifty, with a scale of two. The rate is fifteen, with a scale of three. Multiplying multiplies the unscaled values and adds the scales, so the interest is one hundred eighty thousand seven hundred and fifty, with a scale of five. Every step is whole number arithmetic, so nothing is ever approximated. Then the bank decides how to round. setScale two, with the rounding mode HALF EVEN, rounds to cents, and a tie goes to the even digit, the rule banks use so that rounding errors cancel out instead of piling up. One point eight one. Notice that BigDecimal has no plus or times signs. You call methods: add, multiply. It is a reference type, an object, and Java's operators only work on primitives and strings. Now the warning, at the bottom, from jshell. Build a BigDecimal from the double zero point one, and you get exactly what that double holds, all fifty five digits of it. Build it from the text zero point one, and you get zero point one. So the rule is simple: build money from a String, never from a double.

Ana's account has a number now, SB dash zero zero zero one, stored in a String, and this section looks at strings properly, because a bank is full of them: names, account numbers, references. A String is a sequence of characters, and each one has an index, starting from zero, as the table at the top shows. S is at index zero, B at one, the dash at two. substring three gives back everything from index three on: zero zero zero one, the digits of the account number. The file has a new line too. It uses formatted, which fills each percent s in a template with the next value in order, here the holder's name in capitals and the account number. In the terminal, it prints ANA, account SB dash zero zero zero one. Now the most important fact about strings, and jshell shows it. holder is Ana. holder dot toUpperCase gives back ANA. But then, asking for holder again, it is still Ana, unchanged. A String can never be changed once it is made. It is immutable. Every method that looks as if it changes a string, toUpperCase, substring, strip, replace, actually builds a brand new String object and hands it back, and the original stays exactly as it was. The diagram shows it on the heap: holder still points at Ana, and toUpperCase made a second object, ANA, beside it. Why design strings like that? Because a value that cannot change is safe to share. Many parts of a program, or many threads, can hold the same account number without any of them being able to corrupt it for the others. It is a theme we will come back to when the bank gets its own value types. There is one catch with having many string objects, though. Two different objects can hold exactly the same text, and comparing them the wrong way is one of the most common bugs in Java. That is next.

Here is a bug that has fooled Java programmers for thirty years. Ana walks up to the counter and types her name, and like many people, she adds a space at the end. The program cleans it up with strip, which removes spaces at either end. So login is Ana, and holder is Ana. Are they the same? The program asks twice, in two different ways. The first way, with two equals signs, says false. The second, with the equals method, says true. Look at the diagram to see why. holder points at the String object made from the literal in the source code. strip had to build a new String, because the original had a space in it, so login points at a second object, holding the same three letters. Two equals signs compares the arrows. It asks: are these the very same object? And they are not. The equals method compares the contents. It asks: do these hold the same text? And they do. For primitives, two equals signs compares values, which is exactly what you want: two ints, one and one, are equal. But for any reference type, it compares references. To compare text, always use equals. Why does the wrong version survive so long in real code? Because it often seems to work. Java keeps one shared copy of every string literal in a pool, so two literals that say Ana are the same object, and two equals signs happens to say true. The moment a string comes from somewhere else, typed by a user, read from a file, or built by a method like strip, there are two objects again, and the comparison silently fails. In a bank, that could mean a login that is refused for no visible reason, or a check that lets the wrong account through. The same rule will apply to BigDecimal, to the bank's own types, and to anything that is an object: equals for contents.

The bank prints statements, and a statement starts with a header of several lines: the bank's name, who it is for, and a rule underneath. Building that out of separate strings, joined with plus signs and special newline characters, is fiddly and hard to read. Java has a better way, the text block. It starts with three double quotes and a new line, and ends with three double quotes. Everything between them is the string, line breaks included, so the header in the editor looks exactly the way it prints. The diagram follows it through. First, the compiler removes the indentation. Every line of the block starts with twelve spaces, because the block is indented to sit nicely inside main. Those twelve spaces belong to the code's layout, not to the text, so the compiler strips the indentation that all the lines share and keeps everything else. Second, the line breaks are kept, one per line. And look at the end of the block: the closing quotes sit at the end of the last line, the dashes. That means the string ends right there, with no extra blank line after it. Put the closing quotes on a line of their own, and the string would end with a newline. Then formatted fills in the three percent s placeholders, in order: the bank's name, the holder, and the account number. The table shows each line of the source beside what it prints, and the terminal shows the result: Syndica Bank, Statement for Ana, account SB dash zero zero zero one, and the rule. Text blocks were added in Java fifteen, and they are now the normal way to write any text of more than one line: messages, SQL queries, JSON. We will use them again when the bank starts writing statements and speaking JSON. The header is ready. A statement also needs the transactions themselves, and a day can have many of them.

On a busy day, Ana's account has several transactions: a deposit of twenty five ten, a withdrawal of forty, and a refund of twelve ninety nine. Three variables would work for three amounts, but not for a hundred. Java's simplest way to hold many values of one type is an array. The declaration says BigDecimal, with square brackets, so today is an array of BigDecimal, and the curly braces list its elements. The diagram shows what that builds. The name today holds a reference to an array object on the heap, and the array has three slots, numbered from zero. Slot zero holds the deposit, slot one the withdrawal, slot two the refund. Each slot is itself a reference to a BigDecimal. today square bracket zero reads slot zero, and today dot length says how many slots there are: three. That length is fixed. An array is made with a size, and it can never grow or shrink. Asking for slot three, which does not exist, throws an exception. The file adds the three amounts to the opening balance, one at a time, and the closing balance is one hundred eighteen fifty nine, exactly. Now look at the terminal, at the line after the balance. Printing the array itself gives something strange: an open bracket, a capital L, java dot math dot BigDecimal, a semicolon, an at sign and a number. That is Java's default description of an array: a code for its type, and an identity hash, a number that is different on every run. It is not a bug, but it is not useful either. The line after it uses Arrays dot toString, which visits each element and prints them in brackets, separated by commas. That is the one to use. A fixed size is a real limitation for a bank, where the number of transactions grows all day. Course six replaces arrays with lists that grow. And adding the elements one at a time, by hand, is something the next course replaces with a loop.

The last kind of value in this course is the strangest: no value at all. At the top of the file, outside main, there is now a new variable: String note, a note on the account. It is declared, but nothing is assigned to it. A variable declared there, outside any method, is a field of the program, and a field always starts with a default value. The table shows them: zero for whole numbers, zero point zero for a double, false for a boolean, and for a String, or any reference type, null. null means a reference that points at nothing. There is no object on the heap behind it. The diagram draws exactly that: the note's arrow leads nowhere. Run the file. The statement prints, and then Note colon null. Joining null onto a string is fine: Java simply writes the word null. Then the next line asks the note for its length, and the program stops with a NullPointerException. You cannot call a method on nothing. This exception is so common that recent versions of Java explain it in plain words, and the table takes the message apart. Cannot invoke String dot length: that is what was tried. Because this dot note is null: that is the name that turned out to be empty. Before Java fifteen, the message was usually blank, and finding which of several names on one line was null could take a long time. Now the JVM tells you. Local variables, the ones inside main, work differently: they have no default at all, and the compiler refuses to let you read one before you have assigned it. So most nulls in real programs come from fields, and from methods that return null to mean nothing found. Later in the course, Optional gives the bank a safer way to say that. Remove the note, and the bank can now hold real data, exactly. The next course teaches it to decide, to repeat, and to react to bad input.

The bank can hold data. Now it has to work things out, and in Java, anything that works out a value is an expression. The file computes a year of simple interest on Ana's balance: the balance, times the monthly rate, times twelve months, rounded to cents. With BigDecimal there are no arithmetic signs, so the expression is a chain of method calls, read from left to right: multiply by the rate, then by the months, then set the scale. Running it prints twenty one euros sixty nine. With whole numbers, Java does have operators, and the order they run in matters. In jshell, twelve thousand and fifty plus two thousand five hundred and ten times two. The answer is seventeen thousand and seventy, not twenty nine thousand, because multiplication goes first. The diagram on the right shows the two steps: two thousand five hundred and ten times two is five thousand and twenty, and only then is it added. The table beside it is the rule. Brackets first, then times, divide and remainder, then plus and minus, each level from left to right. Put brackets around the addition, and the answer changes to twenty nine thousand one hundred and twenty. When in doubt, brackets make the order obvious to the next reader, which is worth more than saving two characters. The last two lines in jshell show something every bank programmer needs. Dividing one whole number by another gives a whole number: seventeen thousand and seventy cents divided by a hundred is one hundred and seventy, the whole euros. The percent sign gives the remainder: seventy, the cents left over. Together, they split an amount in cents back into euros and cents. But whole numbers have a limit, and a bank can reach it. That is next.

A business client deposits fifteen million euros, twice, and the bank counts in cents. Fifteen million euros is one billion five hundred million cents, and it fits in an int. Two of them, added together, are three billion. Run the file, and the int version prints a negative number: minus one billion two hundred ninety four million, and so on. No error, no warning. The money simply turned negative. The diagram explains why. An int is thirty two bits, and it can only count up to its maximum, a little over two billion one hundred million. Think of it as a wheel. Add one to the maximum, and instead of stopping, the count goes round to the very bottom of the wheel, the most negative int. jshell shows exactly that: Integer dot MAX VALUE plus one is minus two billion one hundred forty seven million and so on. Three billion went past the top, wrapped round, and landed on a negative value. This is called overflow, and Java, like most languages, does it silently, because checking every addition would cost speed. For a bank, silent is the worst possible kind of wrong. The table shows three ways out. A long is sixty four bits, and the second line of the output shows it holding three billion without trouble: casting one of the values to long first makes the whole addition a long. A long reaches about nine quintillion cents, ninety two quadrillion euros, which is enough for any bank. And when overflow must never pass unnoticed, Math dot addExact does the same addition but throws an ArithmeticException instead of wrapping, as jshell shows. So the rule is simple. An int counts to about twenty one million euros in cents, which is not much for a bank. Count money in a long, or better, in BigDecimal, which has no limit at all. With numbers safe, the bank can start making decisions.

A bank's most basic decision: can this withdrawal be paid? The file asks for two withdrawals in a row, two hundred euros and then forty, against a balance of one hundred twenty euros fifty. Each one goes through an if statement. If the withdrawal is more than the balance, refuse it. Else, subtract it and pay out. The condition in the brackets must be a boolean, true or false, and exactly one of the two blocks runs. The diagram at the top shows the two paths. Two hundred is more than the balance, so the condition is true and it is refused. Forty is not, so the condition is false, the else block runs, and the balance drops to eighty fifty. The terminal shows both. Now look closely at the condition itself, because BigDecimal cannot be compared with a greater than sign. You call compareTo, and it answers with a number: below zero if the first amount is smaller, zero if they are the same, above zero if it is larger. So compareTo greater than zero means the withdrawal is larger than the balance. Why not just use equals to compare money? jshell shows the trap. Two point zero equals two point zero zero? False. equals on a BigDecimal compares the value and the scale, and those two have different scales, one digit after the point and two. compareTo compares only the amount, and says zero: the same. For money, two euros is two euros however it was written, so amounts are compared with compareTo. Notice also that the file repeats the whole if block for the second withdrawal, line for line. Repeating code like that is a sign that something is missing. Two tools fix it later in this course: a loop, to do the same thing for each request, and a method, to give the decision a name. First, though, another way to choose.

Syndica Bank charges a monthly fee that depends on the type of account. Checking accounts pay two euros, savings accounts pay nothing, and business and corporate accounts pay nine fifty. A chain of if and else if would work, but when one value picks one of several results, Java has a better tool: the switch expression. The file switches on the account type. Each case names one or more values, then an arrow, then the result for that case. Business and corporate share one case, separated by a comma. And the whole switch is an expression, so its result goes straight into the variable fee. The diagram shows the matching: the type is checking, so the first case matches, and fee is two euros. Run it, and the fee is taken from the balance: one hundred eighteen fifty. The table lists what makes this form of switch safe. Each case gives one value. Only the matching case runs: older Java switches fell through from one case into the next unless you remembered to write break, and that caused countless bugs. And a switch expression must cover every possible value, or it does not compile. That is what default is for. A type the bank does not know about has no sensible fee, so default throws an exception instead of inventing one. jshell shows the rule being enforced. A switch on a String with only a checking case and no default is refused: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. There are endless possible strings, so without a default it can never be complete. Later in the course, account types become an enum, a type with a fixed list of values, and then the compiler can check that every type has a case with no default at all. Next, doing something for every transaction of the day.

In the last course, the day's transactions sat in an array, and we added them to the balance one at a time, by hand. With four transactions that is tedious, and with four hundred it is impossible. A loop runs the same lines once for every element. The first loop is a for each loop: for each BigDecimal amount in today. On every pass, the name amount is given the next element of the array, and the two lines inside run: add it to the balance, and print the amount beside the new balance. The table on the right follows the four passes. Pass one, twenty five ten in, balance one hundred forty five sixty. Pass two, forty out, one hundred five sixty. Then the refund, and a card payment, ending at one hundred eleven thirty four. The terminal shows the same four lines. Notice the formatting: percent eight s pads each amount to eight characters, so the arrows line up in a column. A for each loop is the right choice whenever you want every element, in order, and do not care about its position. The second loop is the counted for loop, for when the position itself matters. Here it prints the transactions newest first, which means walking the indexes backwards. The table at the bottom takes its three parts apart. The first part runs once: i starts at the last index, three. The second is checked before each pass: keep going while i is zero or more. The third runs after each pass: i minus minus, one less. So i goes three, two, one, zero, and then stops. The loop prints a running number with each amount, i plus one, because people count from one, even though Java counts from zero. These loops know in advance how many passes to make. A teller does not: it serves requests until someone says stop. That is a different kind of loop.

Until now, every run of Bank dot java has done its work and stopped. A teller is different. It waits for a request, answers it, and waits for the next, until it is told to close. This section turns the bank into that kind of program. The loop is while true: a condition that is always true, so the loop would run forever, unless something inside it breaks out. On every pass, IO dot readln prints the prompt, teller, and waits for a line to be typed. Then an if, else if chain decides what the line means, as the diagram shows. If it is quit, break leaves the loop at once, and the program goes on to the line after it, teller closed. If it is balance, print the balance. If it starts with the word deposit and a space, the rest of the line, from character eight on, is the amount, and it is added. Anything else is an unknown command. The table follows the session in the terminal, one typed line at a time. balance prints one hundred twenty fifty. deposit twenty five ten adds the amount and prints one hundred forty five sixty. withdraw ten is not a command yet, so it falls through every test to the final else: unknown command. And quit breaks out of the loop. Notice that the balance survives from one request to the next. It is declared before the loop, so every pass sees the same variable. Declare it inside the loop, and it would be reset to one hundred twenty fifty on every pass. This is the shape of almost every interactive program: a loop that reads, decides and answers. But look at how the chain will grow. Every new command means another else if, with its own parsing and its own printing, all inside main. That does not scale. The next section gives each operation a name of its own.

A method is a named piece of code that does one job. main is a method, and so far it has done everything. Now the teller gets three more. money turns text into a BigDecimal. deposit takes a balance and an amount, and gives back the new balance. withdraw does the same, refusing when there is not enough. Each method declares what it takes, its parameters, in brackets, and what it gives back, its return type, before its name. main gives back nothing, so its return type is void. The loop is shorter too. Instead of an if chain, it splits the line into words, and a switch on the first word calls the right method. The case for deposit reads: balance equals deposit of balance and the amount. Here is what happens when that line runs, and the diagram on the right shows the moment. The call creates a new frame on the stack, on top of main's frame. The new frame holds deposit's own variables: its parameters, balance and amount, and its local variable, after. main's frame is still there underneath, paused, waiting for the answer. deposit adds the amount, prints, and reaches return after. Its frame is then removed from the stack, and the value of after, one hundred forty five sixty, is handed back to main, which stores it in its own balance. That is the call stack: every running method has a frame, the newest on top, and returning removes it. It is the same stack you read in every stack trace, one at line for each frame. The session shows the methods working: a deposit, a withdrawal refused, one paid, and the balance. Notice one detail in the diagram. The balance inside deposit is not main's balance. It is a parameter, a separate variable that starts with the same value. main only changes because it assigns what came back. The next section shows what happens when a method forgets that.

The teller gets one more command, fee, which charges the monthly fee of two euros. Its method, chargeFee, looks perfectly reasonable: it subtracts the fee from the balance and prints the result. But it returns nothing, its return type is void, and it assigns to its own parameter instead. Watch the session. The balance is one hundred twenty fifty. fee says: charged two euros, balance one hundred eighteen fifty. Then the balance is asked for again, and it is still one hundred twenty fifty. The fee was never charged. This is one of the most important rules in Java, and the diagram shows it. Java always passes a copy of each argument to a method. For a primitive, that is a copy of the value. For a reference, like a BigDecimal, it is a copy of the arrow. When main calls chargeFee, chargeFee's balance parameter is a second arrow, pointing at the same BigDecimal, one hundred twenty fifty. Then subtract builds a new BigDecimal, one hundred eighteen fifty, because BigDecimal is immutable, just like String, and chargeFee points its own arrow at the new object. main's arrow never moves. When chargeFee ends, its frame and its arrow disappear, and the new object is simply left for the garbage collector. Some languages can pass a variable itself, so a method can change the caller's variable. Java never does. A method can change an object both arrows point at, if the object has methods that change it, but it can never repoint the caller's variable. And since BigDecimal cannot be changed at all, there is only one way for chargeFee to work: return the new balance, and let main assign it, exactly as deposit and withdraw already do. That is the fix, and it is in the next version of the file. Later in the course, an Account object will hold its own balance, and this problem goes away entirely. Next, what to do when the input is bad.

Ana types deposit, twelve comma fifty, the way amounts are written in much of Europe. BigDecimal expects a decimal point, so new BigDecimal throws a NumberFormatException. Until now, an uncaught exception has meant a stack trace and the end of the program. For a teller, that is unacceptable: one typo, and the bank closes. The fix is a try block around the switch, and a catch block after it. The diagram follows the exception. new BigDecimal, inside money, throws. money stops immediately, its frame is removed, and it returns nothing. Because money never returned, deposit is never even called, so the balance is not touched. The exception carries on down the stack, into main, and main's try block has a catch for exactly this kind of exception: catch NumberFormatException e. The catch block runs, prints not an amount, twelve comma fifty, and then the loop simply goes round again, to the next prompt. The session shows the whole thing. The bad amount is reported. The correct amount, twelve point fifty, is deposited. The table compares the two programs. Without try, the teller stops with a stack trace, and the next line is never read. With try, it says what was wrong and carries on. The e in the catch is the exception object itself, with its message and its stack trace, if you need them. This version also fixes the fee from the last section. chargeFee now returns the new balance, like deposit, and the switch assigns it, so fee takes two euros for real, and the session shows the balance dropping. A catch should be as narrow as possible: catch only the exceptions you know how to handle, here, a number that is not a number. Catching everything would hide real bugs. So far, the exceptions have come from Java's own code. Next, the bank throws its own.

A deposit of minus fifty euros is a number, so it parses perfectly well, and the old deposit would have happily added it, taking fifty euros out. A bank must refuse it. So deposit now checks its input first: if the amount's sign is zero or negative, it throws a new IllegalArgumentException, with a message that says why. throw ends the method at once, just like an exception from Java's own code, and nothing after it runs. withdraw changes in the same way. Instead of printing its own refusal and returning the old balance, it throws, with a message naming the amounts. Why throw, rather than print? Because the method that finds the problem is not the right place to decide what to do about it. deposit does not know whether it was called by a teller, a file import, or a web request. It only knows the request is wrong. Throwing hands that decision back to the caller. Here the caller is main, and main has a second catch, for IllegalArgumentException, which prints refused, followed by the exception's message. The diagram follows deposit minus fifty: the check, the throw, and main's catch printing a deposit must be positive. The session also shows a withdrawal of five hundred refused, and one of twenty paid. Now look at the order of the two catch blocks. NumberFormatException is a kind of IllegalArgumentException, as the table shows: every number format problem is also an illegal argument. Java tries the catch blocks from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. So the narrower one must come first. Swap them, and the compiler refuses, because the second catch could never run. The teller can now decide, repeat and react. But everything about an account lives in loose variables inside main. In the next course, the bank gets real types of its own.

So far, an account has been a handful of loose variables in main: a name here, a balance there, and nothing to say they belong together. With two customers, that is already messy. With thousands, it is impossible. Java's answer is the class, and it is the idea at the centre of the language. A class describes a kind of thing: what it holds, and what it can do. The new file, Account dot java, declares the class Account. It holds two fields, a holder and a balance, and it can do one thing, deposit, which adds to its own balance. Notice the first line: import java dot math dot BigDecimal. Only a compact file like Bank dot java imports the core library automatically. An ordinary class file names what it uses. Since Java twenty two, java Bank dot java finds Account dot java in the same folder by itself, so the program is still run the same way. A class on its own is just a description, a blueprint. new Account builds an object from it, and the diagram shows two: one for Ana and one for Ben, each with its own holder and its own balance, on the heap. Calling ana dot deposit runs the method on Ana's object, so it changes Ana's balance and nobody else's. And notice what has quietly disappeared: the pass by value problem from the last course. deposit no longer needs a balance passed in and handed back. The balance lives in the object, and the method changes the object directly. The terminal shows Ana with one hundred forty five sixty, and Ben with eighty. But look at the last line. main reached into Ben's object and wrote a new balance straight into the field, five hundred less, and Ben now has minus four hundred twenty euros. Nothing in the class stopped it. A class that anyone can write into cannot protect its own rules. That is the next section.

An account has a rule: its balance must never go below zero. In the last section, that rule lived nowhere, so main could break it with one line. Encapsulation means putting the rule and the data together, and then closing the door on everything else. Both fields are now marked private. A private field can be read and written only by code inside the class Account. To fill them, the class gets a constructor, which runs when an object is created; the next section looks at constructors closely. To read them, it gets two small methods, holder and balance, which hand back their values. And to change the balance, there are exactly two ways in: deposit and withdraw, and withdraw refuses an amount larger than the balance. The diagram at the top is the picture to keep: main is outside the class, and the methods are the only ways through the wall to the private balance. That is what makes the rule enforceable. If the only code that can change the balance is inside Account, then you only need to check Account to know the balance can never go negative. Now look at the terminal. main still contains the line that wrote straight into Ben's balance, and this time the program does not even compile: balance has private access in Account, reported twice, once for reading the field and once for writing it. The mistake from the last section has become impossible. The table lists the three levels of access you will use. private, this class only. No keyword at all, the classes in the same package, which for us means this folder. And public, every class. A good default is to make every field private, and to open up only the methods other code really needs. Reading is fine, as the last table shows: balance hands back a BigDecimal, and since a BigDecimal can never be changed, handing it out cannot hurt the account.

A constructor runs exactly once, when an object is created with new, and its job is to make sure the object starts life valid. Account's constructor now checks its arguments before it sets a single field. A holder must not be null or blank. An opening balance must not be below zero. If either check fails, the constructor throws, and the diagram follows what that means. new Account for Chen with minus fifty euros reaches the check, throws an IllegalArgumentException, and the constructor never finishes. So there is no Account object at all, not even a broken one. That is the guarantee worth having: if an Account exists anywhere in the program, it passed these checks. No other code ever needs to ask whether an account's holder might be blank. Look at the assignments after the checks. this dot holder equals holder. Inside the constructor, the plain name holder means the parameter, the value passed in. this dot holder means the field of the object being built. this always refers to the current object, and here it tells the two apart. The class now has a second constructor, too, taking only a holder, for an account that opens empty. It does not repeat the checks. Its only line is this, holder, BigDecimal dot ZERO, which calls the first constructor with a zero balance, so every check lives in one place. Having several constructors with different parameters is called overloading, and Java picks the one whose parameters match the call. main tries all of this. Ana opens with one hundred twenty fifty. Ben opens with nothing, which prints as a bare zero, because BigDecimal ZERO has no decimal places. We will fix how money looks very soon. Then Chen's negative opening balance is refused, and so is an account for a holder made only of spaces. Each refusal comes from the constructor's own message.

Every account needs a number, and numbers must never repeat: SB dash zero zero zero one, then zero zero zero two, and so on. Each account can hold its own number, but the counter that hands them out cannot belong to any one account. It belongs to the bank as a whole. That is what static means. A static field belongs to the class itself, and there is exactly one copy of it, however many objects exist. The diagram shows it: one opened counter on the class, and three objects, each with its own number. Every time the constructor succeeds, it adds one to opened, and formats the new value into the account's number. Notice where the counter goes up: after the checks, so a refused account never uses up a number. The table compares the two kinds of member. opened, and the static method opened that reads it, belong to the class, so you call them on the class: Account dot opened. number and holder belong to each object, so you call them on an object: ana dot holder. A static method has no this, because it does not run on any particular object, so it cannot read a number or a holder. The terminal shows three accounts with three numbers, and the count, three. Two fields also changed in a smaller way. number and holder are now final. A final field must be set in the constructor and can never be changed again. An account's number and its holder are fixed for life. Only the balance changes. Marking everything that should not change as final turns a whole class of mistakes into compile errors. A word of warning: static fields are shared by the whole program, including every thread. When the bank runs many tellers at once, in course eleven, this counter becomes a problem, and we will see exactly why.

In the last course, the account type was a String, and a switch needed a default for every value nobody expected. A String can hold anything: checking, savings, or savngs, misspelled, and nothing would notice until the fee came out wrong. The kinds of account are a fixed list, and Java has a type for exactly that: the enum. AccountType declares two constants, CHECKING and SAVINGS. They are not strings. Each one is an object, created once when the class loads, and they are the only AccountType objects there will ever be. Each carries its terms, too: a monthly fee and a monthly rate, passed to the enum's private constructor and kept in final fields. The diagram shows both, with their fees and rates. Account now takes a type when it is opened. main then does three things with the enum. AccountType dot values lists every constant, in the order they are declared, and the first two lines of output show their terms. Next, a switch on an account's type, with a case for CHECKING and a case for SAVINGS, and no default. That compiles, because the compiler knows the full list, and every constant has a case. If the bank adds a third type later, every switch like this one stops compiling until it is handled, which is exactly the help you want. Then valueOf turns the text SAVINGS into the constant, and ordinal gives its position, one, counting from zero. Finally, valueOf PREMIUM throws an IllegalArgumentException, No enum constant AccountType dot PREMIUM, because there is no such type. Text from outside the program, typed by a teller or read from a file, gets checked exactly once, at the point it becomes an AccountType. After that, the rest of the code can trust it. Enums are perfect for any fixed set: account types, currencies a bank supports, the states a transfer can be in.

Money has been a BigDecimal since the third course, but a BigDecimal is just a number. It does not know it is money, it does not know its currency, and it happily holds a tenth of a cent. This section gives the bank a proper type for money, and Java has a compact way to write it: the record. record Money, BigDecimal amount, Currency currency. That one line declares a class with two private final fields, a constructor that sets them, accessor methods called amount and currency, and equals and hashCode that compare by both fields. The table on the right lists everything that line writes for you. A record is meant for exactly this: a value that is defined by what it holds, and never changes. The block that follows, starting with Money and no brackets, is the compact constructor. It runs before the fields are set, and it can check and adjust the parameters. Here it refuses any amount finer than the currency's cents, and then sets the scale to two digits, the euro's. The diagram follows Money dot eur of ten: scale zero comes in, setScale makes it ten point zero zero, and so every Money is stored the same way. That is why the terminal says that ten euros equals ten point zero zero euros: true. Compare that with BigDecimal in the last course, where two point zero and two point zero zero were not equal. The record also has the methods money needs: plus, minus, times with banker's rounding, and isMoreThan, and each one refuses to mix currencies. toString is replaced, so Money prints as an amount and a currency. It is marked public because the toString it replaces, in Object, is public, and an override can never be less visible. Account now keeps its balance as Money, and Ben's empty account prints as zero point zero zero euros at last. Ana's interest is paid through Money's times. And the last line shows the guard working: a tenth of a cent is refused, so no Money can exist that the bank could not actually pay out.

Two objects can be equal in two very different senses, and a bank has to get this right. main opens two accounts that look identical: both for Ana, both savings, both with one hundred twenty fifty. Are they the same account? The terminal says no, and that is correct. They have different numbers, and a deposit into one must never appear in the other. An Account is an entity: it has an identity of its own, and it is equal only to itself. Account does not define equals, so it uses the version every class inherits from Object, which compares identity, exactly like two equals signs. Money is the opposite. Ten euros is ten euros, whichever object holds it. Money is a value, and its equals compares what it holds, which the record wrote for us. The table at the top puts the two side by side. Now, the part that catches people out. Collections such as HashSet use equals, together with a second method, hashCode. The diagram at the bottom shows how a HashSet finds things: hashCode picks a bucket, and equals checks inside that bucket. So equal objects must have equal hash codes, or they land in different buckets and are never even compared. jshell shows what happens when a class gets this wrong. Key is a class holding an account number, without equals or hashCode. Two Keys with the same number go into a HashSet, and the set holds two of them: a duplicate, because as far as Object is concerned, they are different objects. The same thing as a record, RKey, gives a set of one, because the record wrote both methods, consistently. The file does the same with Money: ten euros, ten point zero zero euros, and twenty five ten make two distinct amounts. The rule is short. If you override equals, override hashCode too. Better still, make values records, and let entities keep the identity they were born with.

Interest at Syndica Bank is about to get complicated. Savings accounts earn one and a half percent a month. Checking accounts earn nothing. And now there is a welcome offer: three percent for the first two months, then the normal rate. Where should that logic live? The answer is an interface. InterestPolicy is a type with a single method, monthlyInterest, which takes a balance and answers how much interest it earns. It says what must be done, not how. Any class can implement it, by providing that method. AccountType now implements it: SAVINGS multiplies by its rate, CHECKING by zero. And a new class, Promotion, implements it too. It pays its own rate while it has months left, and after that it hands the question to another policy, the one it was given. Interface methods are public, which is why both implementations say public. The diagram shows how the pieces fit. An Account has an InterestPolicy, a field holding whichever policy applies, which starts as its account type. It does not know or care which class is behind it. It just calls monthlyInterest. Ben's account is switched to a Promotion with one line, earnWith. The table follows a thousand euros for three months. Ana earns fifteen euros, then fifteen twenty two, then fifteen forty five, as the interest compounds. Ben earns thirty, then thirty ninety, and in month three the promotion ends and he is back on one and a half percent. Why not write a class PromoAccount that extends Account, and overrides how interest is paid? The last table answers it. With inheritance, an object's class is fixed the moment it is created, so a promotion could never be added to an existing account, or end. And every new combination needs another subclass. Holding a policy, which is called composition, lets the behaviour change at run time, and lets policies be combined, as Promotion combines itself with savings. Prefer having to being, as the saying goes.

Everything that can happen to an account is one of a few kinds of transaction: a deposit, a withdrawal, or a transfer to another account. The bank needs each one as data, so it can be recorded, replayed and reported. Transaction dot java declares a sealed interface, and inside it, three records. sealed means the list is closed. Only the types declared here can be a Transaction, and no other code, anywhere, can add one. The diagram shows the whole family: Deposit and Withdrawal hold an amount, and Transfer holds the account it goes to, as well as the amount. Now look at apply, in Account. It takes any Transaction, and a switch decides what to do with it. Each case is a pattern. case Transaction dot Deposit, with Money amount in brackets: if t is a Deposit, take it apart, put its amount into a new variable called amount, and run deposit with it. The table takes the Transfer case apart. Transaction dot Transfer matches only a transfer. Then the brackets take the record apart, and the underscore says we do not need the first component, the destination, here, so it gets no name. The arrow then uses the pieces. These are called record patterns, and they replace a lot of old code that checked types and cast them by hand. And there is no default case. The switch covers every possible Transaction, and the compiler can prove it, because the interface is sealed. The note at the bottom shows what that buys. In a lab copy of the bank, we added a fourth record, Fee, to Transaction, and changed nothing else. Account no longer compiles: the switch statement does not cover all possible input values. Every switch over transactions, anywhere in the code, has to be updated before the bank can run. In the terminal, three transactions are applied in turn, and each record prints itself with the toString the record wrote.

When a withdrawal is larger than the balance, withdraw has been throwing an IllegalArgumentException. But that is the wrong kind of exception. An illegal argument means the caller made a mistake, a bug. Not having enough money is not a bug. It is an everyday outcome that every caller has to plan for. Java has a way to say that: a checked exception. InsufficientFundsException extends Exception, and its message names both amounts. withdraw now declares throws InsufficientFundsException, right in its signature, and so does apply, which calls it. That declaration is a promise the compiler holds every caller to. Any code that calls withdraw must either catch the exception, or declare that it throws it too. The note at the bottom shows the compiler enforcing it. In a lab copy, main calls apply without a try, and the bank does not compile: unreported exception InsufficientFundsException, must be caught or declared to be thrown. So in main, each transaction is applied inside a try, and the catch prints declined, with the reason. The terminal and the table follow the day. A withdrawal of forty is done. A transfer of five hundred is declined, caught, and the loop carries on. A deposit of twenty five ten is done. The diagram shows the two families. Exceptions that extend Exception are checked: the compiler makes sure someone handles them. They are for things that can go wrong even in a correct program, such as insufficient funds, or a file that will not open. Exceptions that extend RuntimeException are unchecked: nobody is forced to catch them, because they mean the code itself is wrong, like an illegal argument or a null. The right reaction to those is to fix the code, not to catch them. The bank is modelled now, with real types and real rules. In the next course, it holds many accounts at once.

A bank's most important record is its ledger: every transaction, in the order it happened, kept forever. An array cannot hold it, because an array's length is fixed, and the ledger grows all day. Java's answer is a List, and the one you will use most is ArrayList. At the top of Bank dot java, outside main, the bank now has a field: a List of Entry, called ledger, which starts as a new, empty ArrayList. Entry is a small new record: the day, the account number, and the transaction. The angle brackets say what the list holds, Entries and nothing else. A new method, post, applies a transaction to an account, and only if that succeeds, adds an entry to the ledger. main posts four transactions for Ana, and the third, a withdrawal of five hundred euros, is declined. So the ledger holds three entries, not four, and the terminal shows them: size three, get zero for the first, getLast for the newest. The side pane shows how an ArrayList grows, because it is worth knowing what you are paying for. Inside, it is still an array, just one with spare room. OpenJDK's ArrayList starts with ten slots, and here three are used. When all ten are full, the eleventh add makes a new array, half as big again, fifteen slots, copies every entry across, and only then adds. The old array is left for the garbage collector. Copying sounds expensive, and once in a while it is. But because the array grows by half each time, the copies get rarer and rarer, and on average adding to an ArrayList is fast. Reading an entry by its position, with get, is instant, because it is just an array underneath. That makes ArrayList the right default list for almost everything. The ledger is in order. But finding one account among thousands needs something else.

A teller types an account number, and the bank must find that account immediately, among thousands. Walking through a list until the number matches would get slower with every account opened. The right tool is a Map, which stores values by key. Bank now has a second field: a Map from String to Account, called accounts, which is a HashMap. A new method, open, creates an account and puts it into the map, under its own number. Then accounts dot get SB dash zero zero zero two finds Ben's account at once, and a deposit is posted to it. The diagram at the top shows how a HashMap finds a key without searching. First it asks the key for its hashCode, a number calculated from the key's contents. That number picks one of the map's buckets, here one of sixteen. Then, inside that one bucket, it uses equals to find the exact key. The table shows the real numbers for our three account numbers, calculated in jshell the same way HashMap does it: the hash code is mixed a little, then reduced to a bucket between zero and fifteen. SB dash zero zero zero one lands in bucket ten, zero zero zero two in bucket five, and zero zero zero three in bucket four. However many accounts there are, a lookup goes straight to one bucket and checks only what is in it. When the buckets fill up, the map doubles its number of buckets and spreads the entries out again. This is why the last course insisted that equals and hashCode must agree: a map is built on both. Two more things in the terminal. Asking for an account that does not exist, SB dash zero zero zero nine, gives null. And the list of keys comes back in the order of the buckets, not the order the accounts were opened. A HashMap promises nothing about order. The null is a problem we will fix with Optional, later in this course.

Sometimes an account needs to be held for review: a suspicious transfer, a missing document. The bank needs a list of flagged accounts, but it is not really a list. An account is either flagged or it is not. Flagging it twice should not put it on the list twice, and the main question anyone asks is simply: is this account flagged? That is a Set. Bank has a new field, flagged, a HashSet of account numbers. The table at the top follows the three adds. add answers with a boolean, telling you whether the set changed. SB dash zero zero zero two is added, true. Zero zero zero three, true. Then zero zero zero two again, and the answer is false: it was already there, and the set still holds two numbers. A set holds each element at most once, by definition. contains then asks whether zero zero zero one is flagged, and the answer is false. That question is where a HashSet really earns its place, and the second table explains why. A HashSet is built on the same buckets as a HashMap: in fact, it is a HashMap underneath, with the elements as keys. So contains goes straight to one bucket, whether the set holds three numbers or three million. A List would have to check every element in turn, one after another. For a bank with a million accounts, that is the difference between one check and a million. So when the question is is it in there, reach for a Set. Notice the order in the terminal, too: zero zero zero three printed before zero zero zero two. Like a HashMap, a HashSet keeps no order. If you need the elements sorted, a TreeSet keeps them in order, at a small cost on every add. Next, a mistake almost everyone makes once, when they try to remove things from a collection while walking through it.

A new account for Dee was opened, but nothing was ever paid in. The bank wants to close every account with a zero balance. The obvious code walks through all the accounts, and removes the empty ones from the map as it goes. Run it, and the loop breaks with a ConcurrentModificationException. It is caught here only so you can see it, and the program carries on. The diagram explains what happened. A for each loop over a collection quietly uses an Iterator, an object that walks the collection one element at a time. The iterator remembers how many times the collection had been changed when the walk started. Inside the loop, accounts dot remove changed the map behind the iterator's back. The next time the loop asked the iterator for the next element, the iterator saw that the count had moved, and refused to go on, rather than risk skipping an element or visiting one twice. That is the exception. The word concurrent is misleading here. Nothing else was running at the same time: concurrent just means while iterating. The fix is the second loop. It uses the iterator directly: hasNext asks whether there is another element, next returns it, and when an account's balance is zero, it calls remove on the iterator itself, not on the map. The iterator removes the element and updates its own count, so the two stay in step, and the walk carries on safely. The terminal shows the map back to three accounts, with Dee's closed. The table sums up the rule: never change a collection inside a for each loop over it, except through its iterator. In the next course, a single method, removeIf, does this whole loop in one line, once we have lambdas to tell it which elements to remove. And when the bank runs many threads at once, in course eleven, a collection changed by two threads is a far bigger problem, which needs collections built for it.

Statements and account lists can be long, so the bank shows them a page at a time. One way would be to write a page class for entries, and another for accounts, and another for every new kind of list. Generics let us write it once. Page dot java declares a record, Page of T. T is a type parameter: a placeholder for a type that is not named yet. The page holds a List of T, its page number, and the number of pages. The static method of, with its own T, takes any list, a page size and a page number, and returns that slice of the list as a Page of the same T. The arithmetic works out how many pages there are, and where this page starts and ends, without ever going past the end of the list. In main, the same class is used twice, as the diagram shows. Page of Entry, for page two of Ana's statement, and Page of Account, for the first page of the account list. Inside each, T is replaced by the real type, so items gives back Entries in one case and Accounts in the other, already typed, ready to use. Before generics, a page would have held plain Objects, and every caller would have had to cast each item back to the right type, and hope. The table shows what T buys. The note shows the best part. In a lab copy, main asks for a Page of Account, but passes it the ledger, a list of entries. The compiler refuses: incompatible types. The mistake is caught before the program can run, instead of as a crash somewhere far away. One surprise about Java's generics: at run time, the T is gone. A Page of Entry and a Page of Account are both just a Page. This is called erasure. It does not matter in practice, because by the time the program runs, the compiler has already checked every use.

The ledger fills up in the order transactions are posted, and posting is not always in date order: a branch sends its transactions late, a card payment arrives a day after it was made. A statement must be in date order. Sorting a list needs one thing: a way to compare any two elements. Entry now implements Comparable of Entry, which means it promises one method, compareTo, answering how this entry compares to another one. The table explains the answer. A negative number means this entry goes first, zero means they are tied, and a positive number means the other goes first. Entry's compareTo uses two keys, as the diagram shows. First, the day. If the days differ, that settles it: LocalDate has its own compareTo, so an earlier day sorts first. Only when the days are the same does the second key matter: then the larger amount goes first. Notice the trick for larger first: it compares the other entry's amount to this one's, the reverse of the usual order. So two transactions are never tied, unless they have the same day and the same amount. For that, Transaction now declares an amount method in the interface. Every record that implements it already has an amount component, and its accessor satisfies the interface automatically. The terminal shows the ledger as posted, with dates out of order, and then after Collections dot sort: the first of October, with the larger amount first, then the third, with forty euros before twelve ninety nine. The table at the bottom shows the result. Comparable defines a class's natural order, the one order that makes sense by default. When you need a different order, by account, or by amount alone, Java uses a separate Comparator, and the next course shows how a lambda makes those one line each. Next, a better answer than null for not found.

In the map section, asking for an account that does not exist gave null, and null is dangerous. Nothing in get's signature warns you it might return null, so the caller forgets to check, and much later a NullPointerException appears, far from the real cause. The bank now has a method, find, that says it in its type. It returns an Optional of Account. An Optional is a small box. Either it holds an Account, or it is empty. The diagram shows both. find SB dash zero zero zero two returns a box holding Ben's account. find SB dash zero zero zero nine returns an empty box. Inside find, Optional dot ofNullable does the conversion: a null from the map becomes an empty box, anything else becomes a full one. The caller cannot simply use the result as an Account, because it is not one. It has to open the box, and that forces the question of what to do when it is empty. The table lists the ways to open it. isPresent asks if there is something inside, and the loop in main uses it: if present, print the holder, otherwise print no such account. get takes the Account out, but throws if the box is empty. orElseThrow does the same, and says so in its name, which makes it the better choice when an empty box really is an error. The terminal shows all of it. Ben is found, zero zero zero nine is not, the balance of zero zero zero one comes out with orElseThrow, an empty Optional prints as Optional dot empty, and orElseThrow on the empty one stops the program with a NoSuchElementException: No value present. In the next course, lambdas unlock Optional's best methods: map, to transform what is inside, and orElse, to give a default. The rule for now: return Optional when not found is a normal answer, and never return null from a method that finds things.

The bank now hands out statements: the list of one account's entries. But a List handed to someone else is a door into your data. If statement returned a list the caller could change, any code holding a statement could add an entry, or remove one, and nothing would stop it. The method statement collects Ana's entries into a new ArrayList, and then returns List dot copyOf of it. copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy: a list that can be read, but never changed. The terminal shows the two things that buys. First, it is a copy. main clears the whole ledger after taking the statement, and Ana's statement still has its two entries. Second, it cannot be changed. main tries to add a deposit of a million euros to it, and the list refuses with an UnsupportedOperationException. The diagram shows the copy: the ledger is emptied, the statement is untouched. The table compares the ways Java gives you a list that cannot be changed. List dot of builds one from the elements you list. List dot copyOf builds a fixed copy of another collection.
