And Collections dot unmodifiableList wraps an existing list in a read only view: nobody can change the list through the view, but the original can still be changed behind it, and the view shows those changes. For a statement, which is a fact about the past, a copy is exactly right. The same idea runs through the whole course so far. String, BigDecimal and Money cannot be changed. Account's number and holder are final. And now a statement is fixed once it is handed out. Values that cannot change can be shared safely, between methods today, and between threads later on. The bank can now hold many accounts and a growing ledger. But building lists with loops and ifs is getting long. In the next course, streams and lambdas say the same things in a line.

The bank now has a real ledger: two accounts, seven entries over two months. Banks are required to review some transactions, and the rules change often, so it helps if a rule can be written down as a value, stored in a variable, combined with others, and handed to code that applies it. In Java, that is a lambda. The first rule says: any single withdrawal of one thousand euros or more. Its type is Predicate of Entry, an interface from the standard library with one method, test, which takes an Entry and answers true or false. The lambda is the arrow expression after the equals sign. The diagram at the top takes a simpler one apart, the second rule. On the left of the arrow, e, the parameter, which will be an Entry. On the right, the body, an expression that works out the answer: is this entry on Ben's account? A lambda is a compact way to write the one method of an interface like Predicate, without declaring a whole class. Look at the first rule's body, too. It uses instanceof with a pattern: if the transaction is a Withdrawal, call it w, and then check that one thousand euros is not more than w's amount. Then the two rules are combined. Predicate has methods of its own, and large dot or isBen builds a third rule that is true when either one is. The loop tests every entry against the combined rule and prints the ones sent for review. The terminal and the table show four: all three of Ben's entries, and Ana's withdrawal of fifteen hundred euros, the only large one. The point is not this particular rule. It is that behaviour has become data. The bank could keep a list of rules, load them from configuration, and apply them all, without the loop ever changing. Lambdas work anywhere Java expects an interface with a single method, and the rest of this course uses them constantly.

Many lambdas do nothing but call one existing method. e arrow e dot account just asks an entry for its account. For those, Java has an even shorter form: the method reference. Entry colon colon account means exactly the same thing. The table on the right lists some pairs. Entry colon colon account for e arrow e dot account. Transaction colon colon amount. Money colon colon plus, for a lambda that takes two amounts and adds them, which the next section uses. And TreeMap colon colon new, for a lambda that makes a new TreeMap, which the section after uses. They are no faster than the lambdas they replace. They are just easier to read, because they name what is done instead of spelling it out. The first line of main's new code puts them to work. In the last course, Entry got a natural order, by day. But a statement printed account by account needs a different order: by account first, and then by day within each account. Comparator dot comparing, Entry colon colon account, builds a Comparator, a separate object that knows how to compare two entries, from the key to compare by. thenComparing, Entry colon colon on, adds a second key, used only when the first one ties. The diagram shows the two keys in order. ledger dot sort takes that Comparator, and the terminal shows the result: all of Ana's entries in date order, then all of Ben's. Entry itself is unchanged. Its natural order is still by day, and any other order can be chosen at the moment of sorting, without touching the class. The last lines show the equivalence directly. A Function from Entry to Money, written as a lambda, and a Function from Transaction to Money, written as Transaction colon colon amount, both give the first entry's amount: twelve hundred euros. Next, the most powerful idea in this course: computing a balance from the ledger itself.

Here is a question that matters in every bank. Each Account keeps its own balance, updated by deposit and withdraw. And the ledger keeps every transaction. If those two ever disagree, which one is right? The answer is the ledger. A balance is just the sum of everything that ever happened to the account, and a stream can work it out. Calling stream on the ledger turns it into a stream of entries, flowing one at a time through a pipeline of steps. The diagram follows Ana's balance through it. filter keeps only the entries for her account: four of the seven go on. map turns each entry into a signed amount, using a small new method, signed, with a pattern switch: a deposit counts as plus, a withdrawal or a transfer as minus. So the stream becomes plus twelve hundred, minus eighty, plus twenty five hundred, minus fifteen hundred. reduce then folds them into one value. It starts from zero euros, and combines each amount with the running total using Money colon colon plus. The result is two thousand one hundred and twenty euros. The terminal and the table compare it with the balance the Account kept: the same, for both accounts. That match is the whole point. The balance can always be derived from the ledger. Banks rely on this. If an account's stored balance is ever lost or doubted, it can be rebuilt by replaying its transactions, and in the next course, Syndica Bank does exactly that every time it starts. Notice how the pipeline reads: keep these, turn them into that, combine them. It says what is wanted, not how to loop over it. The second stream is even shorter: filter the deposits, and count them. Four deposits among seven entries. filter, map and reduce cover a surprising amount of everyday code. Next, splitting the ledger into groups.

A statement is monthly, so the bank needs the ledger split into months: every September entry together, then every October entry. Collectors dot groupingBy does that in one step. A stream ends with collect, which gathers its elements into some result, and groupingBy is a collector that sorts them into buckets. The table in the middle explains its three arguments. First, the key: for each entry, which bucket does it go in? The lambda takes the entry's day and turns it into a YearMonth, a year and a month, such as twenty twenty six, nine. Second, which kind of map to build. TreeMap colon colon new asks for a TreeMap, which keeps its keys sorted, so September comes before October. Third, the downstream collector, what to do with the entries in each bucket: here, simply collect them into a list. The diagram shows the result: two buckets, September with three entries, October with four. The loop then visits each month. For each, it streams that month's entries and folds them into a net amount, exactly as in the last section, but across both accounts. September's net is plus fourteen hundred and twenty euros, money in less money out. October's is plus nine hundred forty four twenty. The terminal shows both. The second groupingBy groups by account instead, using the method reference Entry colon colon account as the key, and the downstream collector is counting, so each bucket becomes a count instead of a list. Ana's account has four entries, and Ben's three. Notice that this time no map was requested, so groupingBy made a HashMap, and the accounts print in no particular order. The same three part pattern, key, map, downstream, covers most reports a bank needs: totals by account type, withdrawals by day, deposits by month. Next, something streams do that loops do not: they do as little work as possible.

Streams have a property that surprises people at first: they are lazy. Building a stream does no work at all. Work happens only when a terminal step, such as count, reduce, collect or anyMatch, asks for the results, and even then, only as much work as that answer needs. The code makes this visible with peek, a step that runs a lambda on each element as it passes, here printing checking and the entry. First, the stream is built, with filter and peek, and stored in a variable. Then main prints built the stream. Look at the terminal: built the stream, nothing checked yet, is the very first line. No entry was looked at when the stream was built, because nothing had asked for one. Then anyMatch is called with the review rule: is there any large withdrawal? anyMatch pulls entries through the stream one at a time, and the table follows it. Entry one, no match. Two, three, four, no match. Entry five, Ana's withdrawal of fifteen hundred euros, matches, and anyMatch stops right there, because the answer is now known: yes. Entries six and seven are never looked at at all. The terminal shows exactly five checking lines. The diagram at the bottom names the two kinds of step. filter, map and peek are intermediate steps: they only describe work to be done. anyMatch, reduce and count are terminal steps: they pull the elements through, and a stream can be used only once, by one terminal step. For seven entries, laziness saves almost nothing. For a ledger of ten million entries, stopping at the first suspicious one, instead of checking them all, is the difference between an instant answer and a long wait. Laziness also means a stream can be built from a source that never ends, and still answer, as long as the question has an answer. So, should everything now be a stream? Not quite. That is the last section.

After a course of streams, it is tempting to write everything as one. Resist that. Some jobs are clearer as a plain loop, and this section puts one of each side by side. The first job is a running balance for Ana's statement: each line shows a change, and the balance after it. The loop keeps one variable, running. For each of Ana's entries, it works out the signed change, adds it to running, and prints the day, the change, and the new balance, formatted in columns. The table on the right shows the result: twelve hundred, then eleven twenty, then thirty six twenty, then twenty one twenty. Every line depends on the line before it. That kind of state, carried from one step to the next, is exactly what loops are good at, and exactly what streams are bad at. A stream processes each element on its own. To build a running balance with one, you have to smuggle the state in from outside, and the result is harder to read and easy to get wrong. The second job is the total paid out, across every account. That is a question about the whole list: keep the withdrawals, take their amounts, add them up. As a stream it reads almost like the question itself: filter, map, reduce. Seventeen hundred euros. As a loop, it would be four lines of setup and an if, hiding the same idea. The table at the bottom sums up the choice. When each step needs the one before it, or when the work is mostly side effects, such as printing, posting or saving, write a loop. When the job is a question about a whole collection, filter it, transform it, total it, write a stream. A stream says what is wanted. A loop says how to get it, step by step. Both are good Java. Pick the one the next reader will understand first. The bank can now report on itself. Next, it learns to remember.

Everything the bank knows lives in memory, and memory is wiped the moment the program ends. A bank that forgets every transaction when it restarts is not a bank. So Syndica Bank gets a journal: a file where every entry is written, one line each, the moment it is posted. The new class is Journal. It holds a Path, Java's name for a location on disk. Path dot of data, journal dot csv names the file, but does not open or create anything; it is just a name. The constructor calls Files dot createDirectories, which makes the data folder if it is missing. Then append turns an entry into one line of text with toCsv, a new method on Entry, and Files dot writeString adds it to the end of the file. The two options say create the file if it does not exist, and append to it rather than replacing it. writeString opens the file, writes, and closes it again, all in one call. The diagram shows post now doing three things: apply the transaction to the account, add it to the ledger in memory, and append it to the journal on disk. Notice that main and post now say throws IOException. Reading and writing files can always fail, a full disk, a missing permission, and IOException is a checked exception, so every method on the way has to declare it or handle it. In the terminal, the bank posts its opening day, and cat shows the journal: three lines, comma separated, the day, the account, the kind, and the amount. The declined withdrawal is not there, because only posted entries are written. The table shows the same three lines. Now look at the second run. It posts the same opening day again, and the journal grows to six lines. The bank wrote everything down, but when it started again, it never read any of it back. Its memory is on disk now, but it still forgets on start. That is next.

A journal is only useful if the bank reads it back. Now, every time the bank starts, before it does anything else, it rebuilds itself from the journal. The diagram follows the start. journal dot readAll reads every line of the file, and Entry dot fromCsv, the reverse of toCsv, turns each line back into an Entry. Then replay applies each entry to its account and adds it to the ledger. It does not append anything to the journal, because these entries are already there. Writing them again is exactly the bug from the last section. Notice one more thing about replay. If a journal entry cannot be applied, say, a withdrawal the balance cannot cover, then the journal itself is wrong, which should never happen. That is not a normal outcome to be handled, it is a broken bank. So replay turns the checked exception into an IllegalStateException, carrying the original as its cause, and lets it stop the program. Only when the journal is empty does main post the opening day, as a brand new bank. The table follows three runs, and the terminal shows them. The first run finds no journal, posts the opening day, and writes three lines. The second run replays three entries, and the balances come back exactly: Ana one thousand one hundred and twenty, Ben three hundred. The third run does the same. And the journal still has three lines, because nothing was written twice. This is the idea from the last course, made real. There, a stream folded an account's balance from the ledger, and the result matched the balance the account kept. Here, the bank does it for everything, every time it starts. The journal is the truth, and every balance is worked out from it. Real banks and payment systems are built this way. It also means the journal must never lose a line. The next section shows how easily it can.

Files dot writeString opens the journal, writes one line and closes it again, for every single entry. That is safe, but slow: opening a file is expensive, and a busy bank posts thousands of entries a minute. The usual fix is to open the file once, keep a writer open for the whole run, and let it collect lines in memory. Journal now does exactly that. Its constructor opens a BufferedWriter, and append writes each line to it. The diagram shows what buffered means. write is fast because it does not touch the disk at all. It copies the line into a buffer, eight kilobytes of memory, and the buffer goes to the file only when it is full, or when the writer is flushed or closed. That last part is the trap. In a lab copy of the bank, main opens the journal and never closes it. The table shows what happens: the first run posts the opening day, the program ends, and the journal has zero lines. Three lines were sitting in the buffer, and when the program ended, they were simply lost. The second run, finding an empty journal, starts the bank over from nothing. Every resource that holds something outside the program, a file, a network connection, a database connection, has to be closed, and closed even when something goes wrong halfway. Java's tool for that is try with resources. Journal now implements AutoCloseable, which means it has a close method, and its close closes the writer. In main, the journal is opened in brackets right after the word try. When the block ends, Java calls close automatically, however it ends: normally, through a return, or because an exception was thrown. You cannot forget it, because you never write it. In the terminal, with try with resources, the journal has its three lines, and the second run replays them. The rule is simple: if a class implements AutoCloseable, open it in a try with resources.

Banks receive transactions from outside: card networks, other banks, an old system being retired. They arrive as files, and files from outside are never quite clean. Syndica Bank now imports a statement, data slash import slash statement dash twenty twenty six dash ten dot csv. Its six rows are on the right, each one beside its verdict. The new class, StatementImport, reads every row and passes it to parse, which runs a series of checks, in order, as the diagram shows. Five fields. A new id, never seen before in this file. A known account. And a positive amount. The first check that fails throws an IllegalArgumentException, with a reason, and the constructor's catch records the row as rejected, with its row number and that reason, and moves on to the next row. Now read the verdicts. T one zero one is accepted. T one zero two, a withdrawal of twelve comma fifty, has a comma inside the amount, so splitting the line on commas gives six fields instead of five. That is the classic European decimal comma, and it is rejected. T one zero three is for account zero zero zero nine, which does not exist. The next row repeats the id T one zero one, the same transaction sent twice, and it is rejected as a duplicate, which keeps it from being paid twice. T one zero four is a deposit of minus fifteen euros, which is not a positive amount. And T one zero five, a withdrawal of thirty, is accepted. The terminal shows the summary: two imported, four rejected, each with its row and its reason, and the two good rows reach the balances. The design choice that matters is this: one bad row must not stop a whole statement. Each row is checked on its own, the good ones go through, and the bad ones come back with a reason a person can act on. Throwing on the first bad row, or worse, quietly skipping it, would both be wrong for a bank.

Interest is paid on the last day of each month. That sounds easy, until you remember that months have twenty eight, twenty nine, thirty or thirty one days. Dates are full of rules like that, and Java's java dot time package knows all of them. The table at the top lists the types this course uses. LocalDate is a day on the calendar, such as the thirty first of October, with no time and no time zone. YearMonth is a whole month. Instant is a single point on the timeline, counted in UTC, the same moment everywhere on Earth. And ZonedDateTime is a wall clock somewhere, a date and time in a particular zone; that is the next section. The new method payInterest takes a YearMonth. atEndOfMonth gives its last day, the thirty first of October, without the bank ever counting days. Then, for every account, it asks how much interest is due. That is a new method on Account, interestDue, which asks the account's policy without paying anything. If the interest is positive, it is posted as a deposit, dated on the last day of the month, through post, so it goes into the ledger and the journal like any other entry. The terminal shows Ana's savings earning seventeen euros eighteen, dated the thirty first. Ben's checking account earns nothing and gets no entry. jshell shows why you should never compute dates by hand. The end of February twenty twenty six is the twenty eighth. Add one month to the thirty first of January, and you get the twenty eighth of February, not the thirty first, which does not exist, and not the third of March: java dot time clamps to the last valid day. And an Instant prints with a Z at the end, for UTC, because it is not a day anywhere in particular. Every one of these types is immutable, like String and Money, so plusMonths gives a new date and never changes the old one. Next: whose midnight is it?

Ana is in New York, and on the last evening of October, at half past eleven at night, she pays for dinner with her Syndica Bank card. Which month does that payment belong to? In New York, it is still the thirty first of October. But the bank is in Europe, and the answer has to be the same every time, for every customer, wherever they are. The code builds the moment exactly as it happened: a ZonedDateTime, the thirty first of October twenty twenty six, at twenty three thirty, in the zone America slash New York. Then toInstant turns that wall clock into a point on the timeline. And LocalDate dot ofInstant asks what day that point is in the bank's own zone, Europe slash Berlin, declared once at the top of the file. The terminal prints all three. Paid at twenty three thirty, minus four hours from UTC, in New York. At three thirty in the morning on the first of November, UTC. Booked on the first of November, in Berlin. The table shows the one instant as three wall clocks. The diagram shows the conversion every bank needs: from where it happened, to the moment itself, to the bank's booking day. So the payment goes on November's statement, not October's, and the code posts it after October's interest has been worked out, so a November payment can never change October's interest. The note at the bottom is the reason a bank never treats a day as twenty four hours. On the twenty fifth of October twenty twenty six, Berlin's clocks went back one hour, at the end of summer time. jshell measures the time between that day's midnight and the next, and Duration says P T twenty five H: twenty five hours. Twice a year, in many zones, a day is twenty three or twenty five hours long. java dot time knows the rules of every zone, so let it do the arithmetic. The bank now remembers. Next, it becomes a real project.

Twelve files in one folder is already too many to find your way around, and a real bank has thousands. Java groups classes into packages, and a package is simply a folder. The bank now has three. ledger dot model holds the bank's types: Account, Money, Transaction and the rest. ledger dot store holds the code that reads and writes files: Journal and StatementImport. And ledger itself holds Bank. The table shows the rule: the folder path under src slash main slash java is the package name, with dots instead of slashes. That long src slash main slash java prefix is the layout Maven expects, and the next sections will show why it was worth choosing now. Every file now starts with a package line, and a class has a full name: ledger dot Bank, ledger dot model dot Account. Look at the top of Bank. Bank is no longer a compact file. It is a class, named in a class declaration, because only a class in the unnamed default package can be compact. Its main is still a plain void main, which any class may have since Java twenty five. And instead of the compact file's automatic imports, it has one line, import module java dot base, which imports every package of Java's core module at once. Then it imports the bank's own classes from the other two packages, one by one. A package is also a border. Package private, the access with no keyword, means visible inside this package only. So to be used from Bank, in another package, Account had to become public, and so did the methods Bank calls, as the diagram shows. What does not need to cross stays behind the border. InsufficientFundsException can only be created inside ledger dot model, by Account. And the compiler found one rule we had not met: a public record's constructor must be public too. In the terminal, javac compiles every source file into a folder called out, and java dash cp out ledger dot Bank runs it.

When the JVM runs the bank, it has to find each class's bytecode somewhere. The classpath is the list of places it looks: folders, and jar files. java dash cp out says look in the folder out. This section breaks that on purpose, twice, to see how classes are found. The diagram shows who does the finding. Classes are loaded by class loaders, arranged in a chain. The bootstrap loader, built into the JVM, loads the core of Java, java dot base: String, List and the rest. Its child, the platform loader, loads the rest of the JDK's modules. And the application loader loads your classes, from the classpath. Each loader asks its parent first, so nobody can replace String with their own. First break: in the terminal, java ledger dot Bank, with no dash cp at all. The application loader looks in the current folder, finds no ledger slash Bank dot class, and the launcher reports Could not find or load main class, caused by a ClassNotFoundException. That exception means: something asked for a class by its name, and it is not on the classpath. Second break: everything compiled correctly, and then Money dot class is deleted from out, as if one file went missing from a deployment. Now look closely at what happens. Bank loads, and starts running. Classes are loaded lazily, the first time they are needed. Only when Bank opens an account, and Account needs Money, does the JVM go looking for Money, and fail. This time the error is a NoClassDefFoundError, caused by a ClassNotFoundException. The difference, shown in the table, is worth remembering. NoClassDefFoundError means the class was there when the code was compiled, and has gone missing since. It almost always points to a broken build or a missing jar, not to a mistake in the code itself. Getting every class onto the classpath, in the right versions, is exactly the job a build tool takes over. That is Maven.

Compiling with javac and a long find command works for one developer on one machine. A real project needs every developer, and every build server, to build it the same way, with the same Java version and the same tools. Java's most widely used build tool is Maven, and a Maven project is described by one file: pom dot xml, the Project Object Model. It is XML, and every Maven pom starts the same way. Then it gives the project its coordinates, shown in the table at the bottom: a groupId, bank dot syndica, an artifactId, ledger, and a version, one point zero. Those three together are the project's name in the world. Any other Maven project could depend on bank dot syndica colon ledger colon one point zero. The properties say: compile for Java release twenty five, and read the source files as UTF eight. Below them, the pom pins the exact versions of the two plugins this step uses, so that every build uses the same ones. Maven does almost all its work through plugins, and pinning them is what makes a build repeatable. Notice what the pom does not say: where the source files are. It does not need to. Maven follows the standard layout, and the bank's code is already in it. src slash main slash java for the code, src slash test slash java for the tests, which the next course writes, and target for everything Maven builds. Convention over configuration: follow the layout, and there is nothing to configure. In the terminal, mvn dash q compile compiles everything into target slash classes, and java dash cp target slash classes runs the bank, exactly as before. The diagram shows Maven's lifecycle, a fixed series of phases. compile, then test, then package. Asking for any phase runs every phase before it, so mvn package always compiles and tests first. You never build a jar from code that does not pass its tests.

Almost no real project is written alone. It uses libraries, other people's code, and in Maven, using a library takes one entry in the pom: a dependency. The bank's first dependency is JUnit, the standard testing library for Java, which the next course uses to test the bank. The dependency gives the library's coordinates, org dot junit dot jupiter, junit dash jupiter, version six point one point three, and a scope: test. When Maven builds, it reads those coordinates and downloads the library from Maven Central, the public repository of Java libraries, into a folder in your home directory, dot m2 slash repository, as the diagram shows. It downloads each version once, and every project on the machine shares it. But one library rarely comes alone. JUnit itself depends on other libraries, and they may depend on more. Maven works all of that out. In the terminal, mvn dependency colon tree prints the full tree, and the table shows it. One line in the pom brought in nine jars: the JUnit API that tests are written against, the engine that runs them, the parameters module, and the small libraries they rely on, such as opentest4j and jspecify. These are called transitive dependencies, and keeping track of them by hand, with the right versions, is one of the main reasons build tools exist. The scope matters too. The table on the right compares the two you will use most. compile, the default, puts a library on the classpath for the code, the tests, and the finished application. test puts it there for the tests only. JUnit is only needed to test the bank, so it is never compiled into the bank's own code, and never ships inside it. If a class in src slash main slash java tried to import JUnit, it would not even compile. Each dependency you add is code you trust and must keep up to date, so add them deliberately.

So far, running the bank has meant knowing where its classes are, and the full name of the class to start. To give the bank to someone else, you want one file that simply runs. That file is a jar, a Java ARchive. mvn package compiles, tests, and then packages the compiled classes into target slash ledger dash one point zero dot jar. The diagram shows what is inside: the bank's class files, in their package folders, and one more file, META dash INF slash MANIFEST dot MF, which describes the jar. A jar is really just a zip file with that manifest inside, which is why the terminal can read it with unzip. The manifest is a list of headers, shown in the table. Which plugin created the jar, and for which Java version. And the one that matters here: Main dash Class, ledger dot Bank. That line is there because of the new configuration in the pom. The jar plugin, pinned to version three point five point one, is told to write the main class into the manifest. Now the bank runs with java dash jar, and the jar's name. No classpath and no class name: the launcher opens the jar, reads Main dash Class from the manifest, and starts it. The terminal shows the bank running from the jar, exactly as before. This is how Java applications are shipped: one jar, which runs on any machine with the right version of Java, on Linux, on a Mac or on Windows, without being compiled again. That is the promise from the first course, compile once and run anywhere, in a single file. One thing to know about this jar: it holds only the bank's own classes. The bank has no runtime dependencies, so that is all it needs. An application with libraries needs them on the classpath too, or packed inside the jar, which is what tools like Spring Boot do. The last course in this chapter adds one more border around the bank.

Packages control what one class can see of another. But public is all or nothing: a public class can be used by any code, anywhere, that has the jar on its classpath. Java's module system, added in Java nine, adds a border around the whole jar. The bank declares itself a module with one small file, module dash info dot java, at the root of its sources. It names the module, ledger, and says exports ledger dot model. That one line decides what other modules may use. In the terminal, jar describe dash module reads the module's description from inside the jar, and the table shows it. exports ledger dot model: other modules can use the bank's types, Account, Money, Transaction. requires java dot base mandated: every module depends on Java's core, automatically. contains ledger, and contains ledger dot store: these packages are inside the module, and nothing outside it can reach them, even though Journal and StatementImport are public classes. And main dash class, ledger dot Bank, which Maven recorded for us. The diagram puts it in a picture: one package exported, two kept inside. The bottom table shows the result. There are now two borders. A public class in a package that is not exported is visible inside this module only. A public class in an exported package is visible to every module. So the journal's file format, and how a statement is imported, are the bank's private business. Another team could build on Money and Account without ever coming to depend on how the journal works, which leaves the bank free to change it. Running a module looks slightly different: java dash p puts the jar on the module path, and dash m ledger starts the module's main class. Java's own JDK is built from about seventy of these modules, which is how the last course will be able to ship the bank with a runtime containing only the ones it uses. Next, the bank proves that it works.

Every course so far has checked the bank by running it and reading what it printed. That works once. It does not work the hundredth time, after a change somewhere else, when nobody remembers what the right output was. Professional code checks itself, with tests: small programs that run the bank's code and confirm the answer, automatically, every time it is built. Java's standard tool for that is JUnit, which the last course added to the pom. Tests live in src slash test slash java, in the same package as the code they test, here ledger dot model, so they can see package private members. AccountTest is an ordinary class. Each method marked at Test is one test, and its name says what it checks: a deposit adds to the balance. The diagram shows the three parts almost every test has. Arrange: build what the test needs, an account holding one hundred euros. Act: do the one thing being tested, deposit twenty five ten. Assert: check the result. assertEquals takes the expected value first, then the actual one: the balance must be one hundred twenty five ten. In the terminal, mvn test compiles the code and the tests, and runs them. Tests run, one. Failures, zero. Build success. Now, the most important thing about a test is that it can fail. In a lab copy, the test expects one hundred twenty five euros instead, and the table shows the result: build failure. The note shows JUnit's message, which says exactly what went wrong: expected one hundred twenty five, but was one hundred twenty five ten. That message is readable because Money has a good toString, which is one more reason to write one. Remember that mvn package runs the test phase before packaging. From now on, a broken bank cannot even be built into a jar. That is the safety net every later change in this course relies on.

Testing that the bank does the right thing is only half the job. A bank must also refuse to do the wrong thing, and those refusals need tests just as much. The second test is about an overdraft. Ben has eighty euros, and tries to withdraw a hundred. The test expects the withdrawal to throw, and JUnit has an assertion for exactly that: assertThrows. The diagram follows it. It takes the type of exception expected, InsufficientFundsException, and a lambda containing the code that should throw it. assertThrows runs the lambda, and catches what it throws. If nothing is thrown, or an exception of a different type, the test fails. If the right exception is thrown, assertThrows hands it back, so the test can look inside it. That is why the lambda matters: if the test simply called withdraw directly, the exception would escape and end the test before any assertion could run. Then the test makes two more claims, as the table lists. The message must name both amounts, exactly as a teller would see it: one hundred euros is more than the balance, eighty euros. And the balance must still be eighty euros. That last check is easy to forget, and it is the one that matters most. A withdraw method that threw the exception after taking the money would pass the first two assertions and still lose Ben twenty euros. Testing what did not change catches that. In the terminal, two tests run, and both pass. Notice how the test reads: a sentence in its name, then a few lines that set up, act and check. When it fails one day, the name and the message together should tell whoever is reading exactly what broke, without opening the code. Next, one test that checks many cases at once.

Back in the third course, the bank chose banker's rounding, half even, for its interest: when an amount falls exactly halfway between two cents, it rounds to the even one. Up to now, that rule has been a claim in a comment. This test makes it a fact. Interest needs many cases checked: ordinary ones, and especially the awkward ones. Writing a separate test method for each would repeat the same three lines again and again. A parameterized test writes the check once and feeds it a table of cases. at ParameterizedTest replaces at Test, and at CsvSource supplies the rows, each one a line of comma separated values. For every row, JUnit calls the method once, passing the values in as its parameters: the balance, the rate, and the interest that should be paid. The diagram follows one row through. The table on the right lists all five. One hundred twenty fifty at one and a half percent pays one eighty one. A thousand euros pays fifteen. Then the three that matter most: each one works out to exactly half a cent. Three cents at fifty percent is one and a half cents, a tie, and it rounds to the even two. Five cents gives two and a half, which also rounds to two. Seven cents gives three and a half, which rounds to four. Always to the even digit, which is how rounding errors cancel out across thousands of accounts, instead of all drifting the same way. In the terminal, MoneyTest reports five tests run, one per row, and seven tests pass in all. The name pattern in the annotation means a failing row will be reported with its own values, so you know at once which case broke. When you find a bug, add its case as one more row. It costs one line, and the bug can never quietly come back.

Some code depends on the time, and that makes it hard to test. Interest is paid on the last day of the month. A method that calls LocalDate dot now to decide whether today is the month end can only really be tested on the last day of a month, and only by luck at the awkward hours. The fix is to stop asking the computer what time it is, and ask a Clock instead. java dot time has a Clock class for exactly this. The new class BankCalendar holds a Clock, and works out today from it, and whether today is the month end. In the running bank, it would be given the system clock in Berlin, which tells the real time. In a test, it is given Clock dot fixed: a clock stopped at one instant, in one zone, as the diagram shows. Now the test can choose any moment it likes, and the table lists the ones it chooses. Half past ten in the evening, UTC, on the thirty first of October is half past eleven in Berlin: the month end. One hour later, half past eleven UTC, it is already half past midnight on the first of November in Berlin. Not the month end any more, and today is the first of November. A system that used UTC by mistake would get that wrong, and this test would catch it. The last test checks February in twenty twenty eight, a leap year: the twenty eighth is not the month end, and the twenty ninth is. In the terminal, all ten tests pass. The same idea applies far beyond clocks: anything a class reads from the outside world, the time, a random number, a file, a network, can be handed to it, instead of fetched by it. Then a test can hand it something fixed. It is called dependency injection, and it is how testable code is written. Next, a record of what the bank actually did.

A bank must be able to say, afterwards, exactly what happened and when: every posted transaction, every refusal. Printing with IO dot println is not enough. Output for the user and records for the operators get mixed together, nothing says how important each line is, and you cannot turn the detail up or down without changing the code. That is what logging is for. Java's built in logging API is System dot Logger, in java dot base. Bank gets one logger, named ledger dot audit. post now logs every posted entry at level INFO, and every declined one at level WARNING, with the account and the reason. replay logs each replayed entry at DEBUG. The table shows the levels, from ERROR, the bank cannot go on, down to TRACE. A logger is configured with a level, and only messages at that level or above are printed. The default is INFO, so DEBUG and TRACE lines are simply dropped, and the replay lines never appear. Turning on DEBUG later is a change of configuration, not of code. The diagram shows where a line goes. System dot Logger is only an interface. Behind it is a backend, which by default is java dot util dot logging, and that writes to the console, on standard error, separate from the program's own output. The first lines of main set the backend's format: just the level, the logger's name and the message. Real logs also carry a timestamp, and this course leaves it out only so that every run prints the same text. In the terminal, the opening day appears as an audit trail: six INFO lines, posted, and one WARNING, Ben's declined withdrawal of five hundred euros. A real bank sends lines like these to files or a log service, keeps them for years, and searches them when something goes wrong. The bank now tests itself and leaves a record. One question is left: what is all this doing to memory?

Every object the bank creates, every entry, every Money, every string split from a line of the journal, takes up memory on the heap. Nobody ever deletes them. Java's garbage collector finds the objects nothing points to any more, and reclaims their memory. This full scene watches it work. Box one is a small lab program. It replays a million ledger entries. For each one, it builds a line of text and splits it into fields, and those strings are garbage almost at once. And it keeps a million Entry records in a list, which live until the end. That mix is typical of real programs, and it is exactly what the collector is designed for. Box two shows how HotSpot's default collector, G1, organises the heap, into generations. Every new object is created in Eden. Most objects die young, like those split strings, so Eden fills up with garbage. When Eden is full, the collector runs a young collection: it copies the few live objects out, into a survivor area, and simply treats the rest of Eden as empty again. That is cheap, because the cost depends on what is alive, not on what is garbage. Objects that survive several collections, like the entries, are promoted to the old generation, which is collected far less often. Box three is the real log, from running the lab with dash X log colon gc, and a heap capped at two hundred and fifty six megabytes. The first line says G1 is in use. Each line after it is one young pause, and the table takes the first one apart: how long the JVM had been running, the kind of pause, how much heap was in use before and after, out of the heap's current size, and how long the program stood still. Box four shows the run: a million entries kept, and the count of young pauses in this run. Each pause takes milliseconds. The exact numbers change on every run, but the shape does not. The bank is tested and understood. Next, many tellers at once.

A real bank does not serve one customer at a time. Hundreds of tellers, cash machines and card payments all reach the same accounts at the same moment. In Java, things that run at the same time run on threads. This course explores them with small lab programs in a new labs folder. Each is a compact file, run with java dash cp target slash classes, so it uses the bank's real Account and Money classes, but none of it goes into the jar. The first lab creates four tellers. new Thread takes a lambda, the work to do, here one deposit of one euro into Ana's account, and a name. Creating a thread runs nothing yet. start does: the new thread begins running its lambda, at the same time as main carries on. Then main calls join on each teller, which waits until that thread has finished. The terminal shows the result, printed only after every teller is done: four tellers ran, main ran on a thread called main, and the balance went from a thousand euros to a thousand and four. The diagram shows the most important fact about threads. Each thread has its own stack, with its own frames and its own local variables. But all of them share one heap. There is only one Account object for Ana, and all four tellers deposit into it. That is the whole point, since they serve the same customer, and it is also the whole danger. With four threads, each making one deposit, the answer came out right. Nothing about this program guarantees it, though. The four deposits happened to run without getting in each other's way. In the next section, a hundred tellers make a hundred thousand deposits, and luck runs out.

Now a hundred tellers each make a thousand deposits of one cent into the same account, which starts at zero. That is a hundred thousand cents, so the balance must end at exactly one thousand euros. Look at the terminal. The first run ends well short of a thousand euros. The program is run again, unchanged, and it ends short again, by a different amount. The table on the right compares them. No exception, no warning, no crash: money simply disappeared, and a different amount every time. This is a race condition, and the table at the top shows exactly how it happens. deposit is one line of code, balance equals balance plus amount, but the computer does it in three steps: read the balance, add the cent, write the result back. Teller A reads five euros. Before A writes anything, teller B also reads five euros. A writes five euros one. Then B, still working from the five euros it read, also writes five euros one. Two deposits were made, and the balance went up by one cent. The other cent is lost. With four processor cores running a hundred threads, steps from different threads interleave all the time, in a different order on every run, which is why the loss changes. Notice why this is so dangerous. The code is correct for one thread. Every test from the last course passes, because the tests are not run by a hundred threads at once. And the bug may not appear at all on a quiet day, then lose money on a busy one. Races are among the hardest bugs to find, which is why the rest of this course is about preventing them by design, not by testing. The first and most direct tool is to stop two threads from doing these three steps at the same time.

The race happened because two threads were inside deposit at the same time. Java's oldest fix is the keyword synchronized. Account's methods that read or change the balance are now marked synchronized. Every Java object has a lock built in, called its monitor. Before a thread can run a synchronized method of an account, it must take that account's monitor, and only one thread can hold it at a time. The diagram shows teller A holding Ana's lock while it deposits. Teller B, arriving at the same moment, is blocked, and waits its turn. When A finishes, the lock is released, and B goes in. The three steps, read, add and write, can no longer interleave. The same lab, unchanged, now ends at exactly one thousand euros, run after run. There is a second, less obvious thing synchronized guarantees, shown at the bottom of the diagram: visibility. Modern processors keep copies of memory in caches, and without some rule, a write made by one thread on one core might not be seen by another thread on another core for some time. The Java memory model's answer is the happens-before rule. Everything a thread wrote before releasing a lock happens before everything another thread does after taking the same lock. So when B takes the lock, it is guaranteed to see the five euros one that A wrote, not some stale copy. That is why balance, which only reads, is synchronized too: a read without the lock could see an out of date balance. Locks have a cost. While one teller deposits, every other teller on that account waits. But it is one account at a time: tellers working on different accounts take different locks and never wait for each other. Next, a lighter tool for the simplest shared values, counters.

Not every shared value needs a full lock. A counter is the classic example, and the bank has one: Account's static opened counter, which hands out account numbers. The lab counts to a hundred thousand three ways, with a hundred threads adding a thousand each. A plain long field, increased with plus plus, comes up short, by a different amount each run, as the table shows. plus plus is read, add, write, the same three steps as the lost deposits. An AtomicLong counts exactly. Its incrementAndGet uses a single processor instruction called compare and swap, shown in the diagram: read the current value, say forty one, and then set it to forty two only if it is still forty one. If another thread changed it in between, the swap fails, and it simply tries again with the new value. No thread ever waits for a lock, and no update is ever lost. A LongAdder counts exactly too, by a different route: each thread adds to its own cell, and sum adds up the cells when asked. When a great many threads are counting and the total is read rarely, that avoids them all fighting over one value, so it is faster. The table at the bottom sums up which to use. Use AtomicLong when you need the current value often, LongAdder when many threads add and few read. Back in the bank's own code, opened was a plain static int, and two accounts opened at the same moment on two threads could have been given the same number. It is now an AtomicInteger, and incrementAndGet hands out each number exactly once. Atomics work for one value. As soon as a change involves two values together, say, money leaving one account and arriving in another, a single atomic is not enough. That is next, and it brings a new kind of bug.

A transfer changes two accounts, and both changes must happen together: money leaves one and arrives in the other, or neither. The new TransferService does the obvious thing. It locks the payer's account, then, while holding it, locks the payee's account, and only then withdraws from one and deposits into the other. Nobody else can touch either account in between. The lab runs two threads at once. One, named ana to ben, moves a cent from Ana to Ben, two hundred thousand times. The other, ben to ana, moves cents the opposite way. The lab is started in the background, and three seconds later, it is still running. It never finishes. jstack, a JDK tool that prints every thread of a running JVM, explains why, and its own lines are in the table: found one Java level deadlock. Each thread is waiting for a lock held by the other. The diagram follows the cycle. ana to ben took Ana's lock first, and now wants Ben's. ben to ana took Ben's lock first, and now wants Ana's. Each holds exactly what the other needs, and neither will let go until it gets what it is waiting for. So both wait forever. There is no exception and no timeout. The transfers simply stop, and the program had to be killed. This is a deadlock, and like the race, it depends on timing. The two threads must each take their first lock before the other takes its second. With a few transfers a day, that might happen once a year, on the busiest day. jstack was able to find this one because it is a cycle of Java monitors, which the JVM can detect, and that is the first thing to run on any Java program that has stopped responding. Detecting a deadlock after the fact is useful. Making one impossible is better, and the fix is surprisingly small.

A deadlock needs a cycle: thread one holds A and waits for B, while thread two holds B and waits for A. Remove the possibility of a cycle, and deadlock is impossible. The trick is to make every thread take locks in the same order. TransferService now compares the two account numbers, and always locks the lower number first, whichever way the money is going. The table shows the result. Before, ana to ben locked Ana and then Ben, while ben to ana locked Ben and then Ana: opposite orders, so a cycle was possible. Now both threads lock SB dash zero zero zero one first, then SB dash zero zero zero two. The diagram follows two transfers that start at the same moment. Both want SB dash zero zero zero one first. Only one can have it. The other waits, while holding nothing at all, so it cannot be blocking anybody. The winner then takes the second lock, does the transfer, and releases both, and the waiting thread goes next. No cycle can form, so no deadlock can happen, however the threads are timed. Notice that the money still moves the right way: the code withdraws from from, and deposits into to. Only the order of taking the locks changed. The same lab, unchanged, now finishes. Four hundred thousand transfers, and the table at the bottom shows the balances: Ana five thousand euros, Ben five thousand euros, and a total of ten thousand, exactly what they started with. Not a cent lost, and not a cent created, which is the one rule a transfer must never break. Account numbers are a natural order for a bank, because every account has one, and it never changes. Any fixed order works, as long as every thread in the program uses the same one. Next: instead of creating threads by hand, let a pool manage them.

Creating a new thread for every job, as the labs have done so far, does not scale. A platform thread is expensive: it has its own large stack, and the operating system has to manage it. A thousand jobs should not mean a thousand threads. The usual answer is a thread pool: a few threads that are reused, job after job. Java's interface for that is ExecutorService. The lab computes month end interest for a thousand savings accounts. Executors dot newFixedThreadPool, four, creates a pool with four worker threads. The diagram shows how it works. Each call to submit hands the pool a task, here a lambda that asks one account how much interest is due. The task goes onto a queue, and submit returns at once. Whenever a worker is free, it takes the next task from the queue and runs it. Four workers chew through a thousand tasks, four at a time. Since a task runs later, on another thread, submit cannot return its answer. It returns a Future instead: a promise of an answer to come. The table explains the calls. future dot get waits until that task's answer is ready, and returns it. So the loop collects all thousand answers and adds them up. The terminal shows the total: a thousand tasks, four workers, fifteen thousand euros of interest. The pool sits in a try with resources, like the journal in course eight. An ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, and its close method waits for every submitted task to finish, and then stops the worker threads. Forgetting to shut a pool down is a classic way to leave a program that never exits. Executors separate what to do, the tasks, from how to run it, the pool, so you can change one without the other. One thing still shared between tellers is the bank's map of accounts. That is next.

The bank keeps its accounts in a HashMap, and with tellers on many threads, many threads will open and look up accounts at once. Is a HashMap safe for that? The lab tests it. A hundred threads each put a hundred different accounts into two maps, a plain HashMap and a ConcurrentHashMap, ten thousand keys in all. Every key is different, so both maps should end up with exactly ten thousand entries. The table shows two runs. The ConcurrentHashMap has ten thousand both times. The HashMap is short, by a different amount each run. Again, nothing was thrown. Inside a HashMap, putting a key means finding its bucket and linking in a new entry, and when two threads do that to the same bucket at the same moment, one entry can simply overwrite the other. Worse things can happen too: a resize at the wrong moment can corrupt the map's structure. A plain HashMap must never be changed by two threads without a lock. ConcurrentHashMap is built for exactly this, and the diagram shows how it stays correct without one big lock. When a key goes into an empty bucket, it uses compare and swap, the same single instruction as the atomics: no lock at all. When the bucket already has entries, it locks only that bucket, so threads working on different buckets never wait for each other. Reading never locks at all. The result is a map that many threads can use at once, almost as fast as a plain one. The bank's own code is changed too: Bank's accounts map is now a ConcurrentHashMap. The java dot util dot concurrent package has many collections like this, for queues, lists and sets, and they should be the first choice whenever threads share a collection. Rather than locking ordinary collections yourself, use one designed for it. Last, a new kind of thread that changes how many there can be.

Most of the time, a bank's threads are not computing anything. They are waiting: for the card network to answer, for a database, for another bank. The lab simulates exactly that. Ten thousand card payments, each of which waits ten milliseconds, as if for the network, and then deposits a euro. It runs them twice. First on a pool of two hundred platform threads, the kind used so far. Two hundred payments can wait at once, so ten thousand need fifty rounds of waiting, and the table shows how long that took. Then on virtual threads, new in Java twenty one: one virtual thread per payment, ten thousand of them, created with Executors dot newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor. The same work finished in a fraction of the time. Both runs deposited exactly ten thousand euros. The exact times change from run to run, but the gap does not. The diagram shows the trick. A virtual thread is not an operating system thread. The JVM runs virtual threads on a few ordinary threads, called carriers, about one per processor core, four on this machine. When a virtual thread has to wait, for a sleep, a network call or a file, the JVM takes it off its carrier, which is then free to run another virtual thread. When the wait is over, it is put back on a carrier and carries on. So waiting costs almost nothing, and a program can have millions of virtual threads. Look at the code: it is plain, blocking code. Thread dot sleep, a deposit, return. There are no callbacks and no special style to learn. Virtual threads help when threads mostly wait. They do not make computing faster: four cores are still four cores. Everything else in this course still applies, too: virtual threads share the heap, so races, locks and ConcurrentHashMap work exactly the same way. The bank can now serve thousands of customers at once without losing a cent. In the last course, it goes live.

Syndica Bank works, but only from its own terminal. To be a real service, other programs have to reach it over the network, and the way almost every service does that today is HTTP, with JSON. The JDK ships its own small HTTP server, in the module jdk dot httpserver, and the bank uses it, so it still has no dependencies at all. module dash info now says requires jdk dot httpserver. The new class Server starts the bank exactly as Bank always has, opening the journal and replaying it, and then creates an HttpServer on port eight thousand and eighty. It registers two handlers: one for paths starting with slash accounts, one for slash transfers. And it gives the server an executor of virtual threads, so every request runs on its own virtual thread, as many at once as arrive. The diagram follows a request. curl, or any client, anywhere, sends GET slash accounts slash SB dash zero zero zero one. The server hands it to the account handler, which finds the account and sends back a small JSON object: its number, its holder and its balance. The JDK has no JSON library, so the bank builds those few lines by hand, which is fine for a reply this small. In the terminal, the bank is started in the background with a small script, bin slash serve. Ana's account comes back. An account that does not exist comes back as an error, with the status code four hundred and four. A transfer of twenty five euros is posted as a form, and the reply says it was paid, with Ana's new balance. And Ben's account shows the twenty five euros arrived. Every transfer writes two lines to the journal, and one small but important change came with the server: the journal now flushes each line straight to disk. A server is stopped, not closed, and the buffered lines from course eight would be lost. Next, a problem every payment API has to solve.

Networks fail in an awkward way. A client sends a transfer, the bank pays it, and then the reply is lost on its way back. From the client's side, it looks exactly like a request that never arrived. The only sensible thing for the client to do is to send it again. The table on the right shows what that does today. A transfer of twenty five euros is sent, and paid. The same transfer is sent again, as a retry, and paid again: Ana's balance drops twice. To the bank, two identical requests are two transfers. That is the failure, and it is real, in the terminal. The standard fix is an idempotency key. The client invents a unique key for each payment it means to make, and sends it in a header, Idempotency dash Key. The bank remembers every key it has seen, together with the reply it gave. The diagram shows the two cases. A new key: make the payment, and store the reply under the key. A key seen before: make no payment, and send back the stored reply, exactly as it was. In the code, done is a ConcurrentHashMap from keys to replies, and the whole rule is one call: computeIfAbsent, key, then pay. computeIfAbsent runs pay only if the key is not already there, and it does that atomically, so even two retries arriving at the same moment, on two virtual threads, cannot both pay. Requests without a key work as before, with no protection. Back to the table. The transfer sent with key t dash seven is paid, and Ana has one thousand and eighty seven twenty eight. The retry with the same key gets the same reply, with the same balance: nothing was paid twice. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. A real bank would keep keys in its database and expire them after a day or so. Next, the client's side.

curl is fine for trying an API, but most clients of a bank are other programs. Java has a modern HTTP client built in, java dot net dot http dot HttpClient, and this lab uses it to test the whole bank at once. The diagram shows one call. An HttpRequest is built, with a URI, any headers, and a body. client dot send sends it and waits for the reply, which is perfectly fine on a virtual thread, because waiting is what virtual threads are cheap at. The HttpResponse that comes back has a status code and a body. The lab first gets Ana's account. Then it starts a hundred payments of one cent each, from Ana to Ben, on virtual threads, all at the same time. And it sends every one of them twice, both with the same idempotency key, pay dash zero up to pay dash ninety nine, exactly as a client that retried every request would. That is two hundred requests arriving at the server at once. The table at the bottom shows what each key does: the first send pays, the second gets the stored reply. Then the lab gets Ana's account again. The table in the middle compares the two balances: before, and after. The difference is exactly one euro: a hundred payments of one cent, each paid once, and none paid twice, even though every one was sent two times, concurrently. This is the whole course working together in one run. Virtual threads send the requests, and the server handles them on virtual threads. The idempotency keys stop the double payments. TransferService's ordered locks keep the two accounts consistent, and synchronized keeps every cent of every balance. The tests from course ten check the parts, and this lab checks the whole. Testing a running service from the outside, with real requests, is called an end to end test. Next, getting the bank onto a server.

To run the bank on another machine, that machine needs Java. Installing a whole JDK on a server, with its compiler, its tools and all its modules, just to run one application, is a lot of extra weight. Because the bank is a module, which says exactly what it requires, Java can build it a runtime of its own. jlink takes the bank's module, follows its requires to the end, and writes a new runtime folder containing only the modules that are actually needed. The terminal lists them, and so does the table: java dot base, jdk dot httpserver, and ledger itself. Three modules, instead of the JDK's sixty nine. The size table shows what that saves: the runtime folder, beside the full JDK it was built from. The runtime is a complete Java, with its own bin slash java, and the bank's code inside it, so it runs with no Java installed on the machine at all. It is also the natural thing to put into a container image, which is how most services are deployed today. The other change in this section is configuration. A service must not have its settings built into the code. The same build should run on a laptop, a test server and in production, each with different settings. So Server now reads its port from a system property, ledger dot port, with eight thousand and eighty as the default. In the terminal, the jlink runtime starts the bank with dash D ledger dot port equals nine thousand and ninety, and curl reaches Ben's account on that port. Nothing was rebuilt. System properties and environment variables are the simplest forms of configuration. Real services add configuration files and secret stores, but the rule is the same: settings come from outside. The bank is finished. The last section looks at where to go next.

Syndica Bank started as one file that printed one balance with a lost zero. It ends as a tested, packaged service, with exact money, real types, a journal that survives a restart, ten thousand concurrent transfers without a lost cent, and an API where a retried payment pays once. Every part of it was built with nothing but the JDK, and every output in this course came from really running the code. Real banks are built from the same ideas, with bigger tools, and this map pairs each part you built with the tool that does its job at scale. The HTTP server becomes Spring Boot, the most widely used framework for Java services, which brings routing, JSON, validation and security, and runs happily on the virtual threads you already understand. The journal, an append only log of every event, replayed to rebuild state, is exactly the idea behind Apache Kafka, which many services share as their event log. The accounts in a map become tables in a database such as PostgreSQL, usually reached through JPA, which maps Java objects to rows. The JUnit tests grow into tests that start a real database with Testcontainers. And the jlink runtime goes into a container image, so the bank runs the same everywhere. None of these tools will feel like magic now. Spring's request handlers are your account and transfer handlers. Its transactions are your synchronized blocks and your ordered locks. Kafka is your journal, shared. When something goes wrong, you can read the stack trace, the deadlock report, and the GC log, because you have seen each one, on purpose, in this course. The best next step is to build something of your own, the way the bank was built: one small feature at a time, run every time, with tests that keep it honest. Thank you for building Syndica Bank.
